  8 words for intermediate students
  1) Enhance
  To improve something or make it better
  2) Contribute
  To give something time $, energy to help achieve a goal or benefit
  3) Adapt
  To change or adjust in response to new conditions
  4) Efficient
  Somethings woks well without wasting time or effort
  5) Convey 
  To communicate or make known
  6) Furthermore
  In addition; more importantly
  7) Consequently 
  Indicating cause-effect, relationship
  8) Converserly
  Introducing an opposite of contrasting idea
  
  Spice up your english

  04:00 🔄 Vocabulary expansion with 'efficient' and 'convey'
  - Discusses 'efficient', relating to performing in the best possible manner with least waste of time and effort, and 'convey', to communicate or make known effectively.
  05:33 🔗 Advanced vocabulary with 'furthermore' and 'consequently'
  - Teaches 'furthermore', used to add more information or to say something in addition, and 'consequently', indicating a cause and effect relationship.
  06:43 🔄 Wrapping up with 'conversely'
  - Introduces 'conversely' to suggest a contrast or an alternative perspective, completing the list of eight vocabulary words.

      Unfortunately you are right. I would say that in German simple past and present perfect are pretty much used interchangeably. Simple present is often used instead of simple future too. You might hear "I go to the shop" instead of "I will go to the shop". At the same time past perfect or future perfect will be used by pretty much nobody except by somebody who is bad with tenses and uses them by accident.
      
      But for what it's worth: My mom always used to say: "Just because somebody jumps off a cliff, it doesn't mean you should do so too" and "just because everybody does it, it doesn't necessarily make it right." 
      So if you are sure that you use the tenses correctly, use it. It might even encourage some native speakers to think about their use of their language.
      
      Just an example for how terribly wrong natives can be: A popular "news"paper in Germany once asked about some politician: "Can (person) chancellor?" This question is used to this day especially in the media. It isn't even a proper sentence.

**@rybinvital** (👍0 · 2024-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eJF-sXujcVg&lc=UgwvAP9T30LZ9GuVCx14AaABAg
  I think in the past simple tense when we are dealing with a continuous in time action we have to use a "time container" instead of the exact time point, which contains the whole described action in it - from the action's beginning till its end. 
  
  For example, when we use 'yesterday', we imply that the whole action described by a verb phrase - from its beginning till its end - lays inside 'yesterday'. More strictly the action started after yesterday had started and ended before yesterday's end. The action mentioned cannot start earlier - a day before yesterday - and cannot end after yesterday's ending (today).
  
  That means we are selecting a time period (instead of exact point in time) big enough to contain inside it the whole time period of an action's life.
  
  It's like putting smaller "action's time container" into a bigger "time container" - similar to the Russian 'matrioshka' toy principle.
  
  P.S. Even when we use time marker like 'five hours ago', we imply a "one hour time container" beginning in time point 'six hours ago' and ending in time point 'five hours ago'. 
  
  P.P.S. When we are dealing in the past simple with instantaneous events - actions taking less than a few seconds like jumping, sneezing or shooting - we are talking about the exact point in time, as we treat such events not like 'time containers'  having some time length of its life but rather as points in time with zero length in time.

    ↳ **@EnglishwithVahid1** (👍1 · 2024-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eJF-sXujcVg&lc=UgzyiabiiEgzahI_aAx4AaABAg.A3Lijl3sQP5A3YlUxx0Ehr
      The past perfect tense shows that one action happened before another in the past.
      
      :
      Examples:

  🎯 Key Takeaways for quick navigation:
  00:00 📚 E is studying business phrasal verbs for a new job.
  00:54 🏟️ "Kick off" means to start something, like a new product or a meeting.
  01:52 🖌️ "Brush up on" is to update or improve a skill, like learning a language.
  02:45 👎 "Turn down" means to reject or say no to something, like a job offer.
  04:10 ❌ "Fall through" means something doesn't happen as planned, like a deal not going through.
  05:04 💵 "Bank on" means to trust that something will happen, like relying on someone's skills.
  06:00 🗣️ "Ask around" is to get opinions from different people to gather information.
  07:25 🎯 "Zero in on" means to focus closely on something specific, like studying phrasal verbs for business.
  09:14 🤔 Understanding context is crucial for choosing the correct phrasal verb in sentences.
  16:59 📝 Homework questions to practice phrasal verbs.

  🎯 Key Takeaways for quick navigation:
  00:00 📚 The lesson is about prepositions of time.
  01:22 🌧️ "Throughout" refers to a period of time from the beginning to the end.
  02:13 ⏰ "Out of" means to be out of time or to use up all the available time.
  03:01 ⏳ "Around" or "about" are used for approximate times.
  04:20 🤔 The difference between "around" and "at around" is subtle and context-dependent.
  05:16 🌟 "During" indicates a part of a larger period of time when something occurs.
  06:42 🕓 "Ahead of" means to come early or be in front of someone/something.
  07:07 🕰️ "Within" indicates something happening between now and a specified length of time.
  07:59 🌐 "Between" refers to something happening after one time but before another time.
  14:11 🕗 "By the time" means before a specified time.
  14:37 📍 "On the dot" refers to something happening exactly at a specific time.
  15:04 ⏱️ "Just in time" indicates finishing or arriving at the last possible moment.

**@user-xg3kx1zk4r** (👍0 · 2023-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=R1pzn5dS4_o&lc=Ugznpzb-NUOy94LPApN4AaABAg
  Hello! I propose to stop using the ending -s in Present Simple. At least we can use it optionally. Actually we don't need to use it in singular verb forms because -s is first of all an indicator of PLURAL for substantives (book - books, house - houses etc.) That's why it don't associate with a meaning of "singularity". Therefore "he makes" for example sound illogically. He/she/it is ONE person/subject, that's why he/she/it don't need -s. We should say "he make" like we do it for other verb forms (I make, you make, they make) as well as in Past Simple - all verb forms are the same for each person (I made, you made, he made etc.) It really make the system of verbs clear, well balanced and not confusing. Nowadays, this abundant ending is really unnecessary, becoming more and more a kind of obsolete rudiment. Any way, the most of foreign learners don't like this ending and they often forget to use it, having unconsciously a feeling an -s in the 3rd person SINGULAR seem to be something unnatural.

  1. Read
  Think of a similar word
  Learn the pronunciation
  Write down new words with its meaning
  Look for related words (adj, noun, verb, etc)
  Look for its antonym or a synonym of a word
  
  2. Watch TV, movies or online videos
  Watch with your notebook
  Practice out loud
  Pay attention to pronunciation (imitate)
  
  How to memorize everything?
  Try to memorize 3-5 words day.
  Tip 1. The Laura
  Add a melody to the information or words (Make a song)
  Tip 2. Repetition and grouping
  Organize your words or information
  Tip 3. Visualization

  Hi! I found many of your videos useful, especially because of their focus on pronunciation, which definetely is the most difficult aspect of this language, in my opinion. Regarding how to improve the vocab, well I think I have a good tip: MUSIC.
  What I personally do is trying to understand the lyrics the best I can, but when a song is particularly tough to understand (great!) I download the lyrics. Then I copy them and I delete some of the words, so the next time I listen to the song I will play the game of filling the gaps. Of course I also sing along, which is great for pronunciation. I think this works better than movies. And that's because it's very hard to enjoy a movie with many pauses to jot down words or sentences. And in the end you don't do it. Music, instead, gives you the opportunity to listen to the same language input over and over again without getting bored. And you get a lot of phrasal verbs and idioms in context! If you love music as much as I do, you will improve your english and really enjoy the songs you listen to.
  Greetings from Italy!

  Many times I find myself not knowing how to use a word that I know or how to say a phraze or how to finish a sentence because I did wrong that I used to learn a direct translation of separate words instead of perhaps learning the whole sentences. Now I'm trying to replace everything I mentaly say to myself with an english alternative. I watch short videos of a person talking about some stuff on youtube and repeat every sentence word by word to get used to the way people express themselves. I sometimes slow down the video to listen to syllables how they should sound naturally. I keep in mind that there doesn't have to be an exact translation for what I want to say so I need to find out what people would say instead. Individual words probably don't mean the same thing that appears in the dictionary because they get used differently in other situations. Therefore I strive to use english explanation glossary as much as possible rather than using only a simple dictionary. We should get used to expressing all thoughts differently - the English way.

  Ok, here I tell you, how I've learned roundabout 10.000 English vocabularies....
  
  1. I have written a storage program in Excel VBA (visual basic application), where I stored and organised new vocabularies from books I've read.
  
  
  2. When I read a new book, I entered new vocabulaies into my Excel database, with example-sentences and a scorefield for nowledge with the marks 6,5,4,3,2,1 . 6 meant no clue-new word and 1 meant, that I know the word very good.
  
  On each learning session, I took about 20 vokabulary and gave them new score marks. If they reached the score 2 or 1 then they were finished. By this 'system' I learned all new new words.

  Quixotic comes from Don Quixote, which was a philosophical book where one of the characters was a noble knight with a few screws loose that jousted Windmills believing they were giants. Quixotic is connected to that knightly character, describing someone chasing a cause or ideal that is not worth chasing… but you can’t help but admire their earnest dedication towards their misguided crusade. It’s also where the idiom “tilting at windmills” comes from, in reference to the knight jousting the windmills; it’s often used as a criticism because throwing yourself at a windmill for reasons that only make sense to you makes you look like a fool to everyone else. But you are so convinced of the righteousness of your actions that you will do it anyway, just like the knight tilting at windmills because they think it is the right thing to do.

**@kkjnaim5880** (👍304 · 2025-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UgsZLtBru30&lc=UgwGdkVHI9X0phKMjYt4AaABAg
  1. Proponent: A person who supports or argues for something. 
  
  She is a proponent of renewable energy.
  
  
  
  2. Solely: Only or exclusively.
  
  The project is solely his responsibility.
  
  
  
  3. Decade: A period of 10 years.
  
  They have been friends for over a decade.
  
  
  
  4. Abundant: More than enough; plenty.
  
  There was an abundant supply of food at the event.
  
  
  
  5. Roughly: Approximately; not exactly.
  
  There are roughly 50 people in the room.
  
  
  
  6. Conquer: To overcome or take control of something, often by force.
  
  The explorers set out to conquer the mountain.
  
  
  
  7. Vulnerable: Open to attack or harm.
  
  The animal was vulnerable to predators without its herd.
  
  
  
  8. Taxonomy: The classification of something, especially organisms.
  
  In biology, taxonomy helps us organize different species.
  
  
  
  9. Debris: Scattered fragments or remains, especially from something destroyed.
  
  After the storm, debris was scattered across the streets.
  
  
  
  10. Sustainability: The ability to maintain or support something over time.
  
  Sustainability is key to preserving natural resources.
  
  
  
  11. Amateur: A person who engages in a pursuit, especially a sport, on an unpaid basis.
  
  He’s an amateur photographer but takes great pictures.
  
  
  
  12. Foster: To encourage or promote the growth of something.
  
  They fostered a love for reading in their children.
  
  
  
  13. Likewise: In the same way; similarly.
  
  She studied hard, and I will do likewise.
  
  
  
  14. Deploy: To position or arrange something for use.
  
  The company will deploy new resources to the project.
  
  
  
  15. Tackle: To deal with or handle a problem.
  
  We need to tackle the issue of climate change.
  
  
  
  16. Redundant: Not needed or more than necessary.
  
  The extra details in the report are redundant.
  
  
  
  17. Apparently: As far as one knows; seemingly.
  
  Apparently, the meeting was canceled.
  
  
  
  18. Contaminate: To make something impure by exposure to or addition of a harmful substance.
  
  The water was contaminated by chemicals.
  
  
  
  19. Steer away from/Steer clear of: To avoid something.
  
  You should steer clear of unhealthy foods.
  
  
  
  20. Otherwise: In a different way or under different circumstances.
  
  You must hurry, otherwise, you'll be late.
  
  
  
  21. Assess: To evaluate or estimate the nature or quality of something.
  
  The teacher will assess the students' work.
  
  
  
  22. Compile: To gather or put together information.
  
  She compiled a list of her favorite books.
  
  
  
  23. Property: A quality or characteristic of something; also refers to ownership of land or belongings.
  
  One property of water is that it freezes at 0°C.
  
  
  
  24. Generate: To produce or create something.
  
  The wind turbines generate electricity.
  
  
  
  25. Threat: A danger or something likely to cause harm.
  
  Climate change poses a threat to the environment.
  
  
  
  26. Target: A goal or something aimed at.
  
  Our sales team has a target of selling 500 units.
  
  
  
  27. Vigorous: Strong, energetic, and active.
  
  He took a vigorous walk every morning.
  
  
  
  28. Guideline: A general rule or piece of advice.
  
  The company follows strict safety guidelines.
  
  
  
  29. By-product: Something produced in addition to the main product.
  
  Cheese is a by-product of milk production.
  
  
  
  30. Promote: To help something grow or advance.
  
  They promote healthy eating habits at school.
  
  
  
  31. Outbreak: A sudden occurrence of something, typically a disease.
  
  The outbreak of flu spread quickly through the town.
  
  
  
  32. Retention: The ability to keep or hold something.
  
  Employee retention is important for company stability.
  
  
  
  33. Abide by: To follow or adhere to something.
  
  You must abide by the rules of the game.
  
  
  
  34. Resilience: The ability to recover quickly from difficulties.
  
  She showed great resilience after the accident.
  
  
  
  35. Decline: To decrease or become smaller in amount or quality.
  
  The company's profits declined last year.
  
  
  
  36. Foreseeable: Something that can be predicted or expected.
  
  We don’t expect any major changes in the foreseeable future.
  
  
  
  37. Outline: To give a general description or summary of something.
  
  He outlined the key points of the proposal.
  
  
  
  38. Stem from: To originate from or be caused by something.
  
  Her success stems from years of hard work.
  
  
  
  39. A range of: A variety of different things.
  
  The store offers a range of products.
  
  
  
  40. Database: A structured set of data held in a computer or online.
  
  We store all our customer information in a database.
  
  
  
  41. Out: Not in a specific place or situation; absent.
  
  The lights went out during the storm.
  
  
  
  42. Enormously: Greatly or to an extremely large degree.
  
  The project was enormously successful.
  
  
  
  43. Designate: To officially choose someone or something for a specific purpose.
  
  She was designated as the team leader.
  
  
  
  44. Incorporate: To include something as part of a larger whole.
  
  We need to incorporate these changes into the report.
  
  
  
  45. Literate: Able to read and write; knowledgeable in a specific area.
  
  She is computer-literate and handles all the technical tasks.
  
  
  
  46. Correlate: To have a mutual relationship or connection.
  
  The data correlates with the study’s findings.
  
  
  
  47. Years to come/Generations to come: In the future, often far ahead.
  
  This decision will affect generations to come.
  
  
  
  48. Congestion: Overcrowding, often in traffic or the respiratory system.
  
  Traffic congestion is a big problem in cities.
  
  
  
  49. Timber: Wood prepared for building or carpentry.
  
  The house was built using high-quality timber.
  
  
  
  50. Collision: A crash or conflict between two things.
  
  There was a collision between two cars on the highway.
  
  
  
  51. Habitat: The natural environment where a species lives.
  
  The rainforest is the habitat of many exotic animals.
  
  
  
  52. Issue: A problem or topic of concern.
  
  The meeting focused on the issue of climate change.
  
  
  
  53. Cope with: To handle or manage something difficult.
  
  She found it hard to cope with the stress of work.
  
  
  
  54. Preserve: To protect or keep something in its original state.
  
  We must preserve our historical landmarks for future generations.

  54 words or 55 as i recorded????
  1 Proponent (A person who argues for a cause or proposes an idea or in favour of an idea)
  2- Opponent (person who is against of an idea or proposal)
  3-Solely (Only)
  4-Decade (Period of 10)
  5-Abunant (present in large quantity- a region with abundant natural resources)
  6- Roughly(approximately, about- roughly 2000, about 2000)
  7-Conquer(To defeat someone or something , usually by force- you can conquer physical challenges)
  8-Vulnerable / Susceptible (vulnerable person is someone who easily hurt, attacked, influenced)
  9-Taxonomy (The process of classifying living things, organizing them according to their similarities - The taxonomy of species, system for naming and organizing things in groups that share similar qualities)
  10-DEBRIS(Trash, scatter around after disaster)
  11- SUSTAINABILITY (The ability of something to last - As a civilization we are concerned about the sustainability of our planet - environmental or ecological sustainability) 
  12-Amature (is the person who does something for pleasure, not for money)
  13- FOSTER (To encourage of development or growth of something- relationship,skils, ideas- foster innovation, unity,collaboration )
  14-LIKEWISE(Similarly )
  15-DEPLOY(Bringing something into effective action- use utilize-employ, exploit - A company might deploy  new technology to improve efficiency  )
  16-Tackle( To make a determined effort to deal with a problem or difficult task
  17- Redundant(No longer needed or useful)
  18- Apparently (Adverb- Evidently or obviously- apparently true, apparently not)
  19- CONTAMINATE(To make poisonous, to pollute- chemical can contaminate water supplies)
  20- Steer away from / Steer clear of (To avoid someone or something- Her speech steered clear of controversial issues / He decided to steer away from trouble)
  21-Otherwise (You had better write it down, otherwise you will forget it / differently, in other way- The police believe he is the thief but all the evidences suggests otherwise )
  22-Assess ( To evaluate)
  23-Compile (To gather information from different sources and put it together)
  24- PROPERTY (belongs to some one or speciality - one of the properties of copper is that it conduct heat and electricity very well)
  25- Generate (To produce or create something)
  26- Threat (A person or thing is likely to cause damage or danger - climate change is a global threat)
  27- TARGET (sales target, targeted audience )
  28-VIGOROUS (Strong, Healthy, full of energy )
  29- Guidleines (General rules, principles or piece of advice) 
  30- By - Product(something produced in the process of making something else)
  31-Promote (to support, or actively encourage something, a cause, product, idea)
  32 - Outbreak ( A sudden occurrence of something undesirable, conflict, a disease )
  33- Retention(The ability to keep or hold something- the continue use, existence, or possession of something or someone- heat retention - water retention - information retention)
  34 - Abide By ( to accept and follow a rule, decision, recommendation)
  35 - Resilience ( The ability to recover quickly from difficulties - A resilient community is the one that can rebuild itself quickly after a disaster)
  36- Decline (To decrease in, strength, quality, importance)
  37-Foreseeable(if you know something is coming in future it is foreseeable- near or predictable future)
  38- Outline (Summary of main points or structure - you can outline a plan, outline steps, outline proposal- a teacher might outline the key topic for exam, to roughly describe)
  39- Stem from ( To be caused by something or someone or to come from something or someone -Her problem stem from a lack of confidence)
  40- A Range of (a variety of, a diversity of, an array of)
  41 - Database (The police use database to track criminals)
  42 - Ultimately (in the end, finally)
  43 - Enormously(Greatly or to a very large degree, enormously successful, enormously popular, enormously important)
  44-Designate(to officially choose someone to do a job)
  45- Incorporate (to include or integrate a part into the whole
  46-Literate (able to read and write, computer literate, highly literate)
  47-Correlate (To have mutual relationship or connection between two or more things, Higher education levels correlate with better job prospects)
  48-Years to come / Generations to come(coming years / next generations)
  49-Congestion (Traffic congestion, overcrowding)
  50 - Timber(wood used for construction) 
  51-Collision (accident, crash)
  52-Habitat( Natural environment, natural home)
  53 - Issue (broblem)
  54 - Cope with (To deal effectively with something difficult like stress, challenges,  changes - He is trying to cope with being fired so soon after being hired)
  55- Preserve(to keep something as it is)

  Solely - only 
  Roughly - approximately 
  Conquer - defeat something / fight something 
  Vulnerable - easily influenced or attacked or hurt 
  Taxonomy - classifying / organizing according to their similarities 
  Debris - trash scattered around after a disaster  
  Sustainability - ability of sth to last 
  Foster - to encourage the development 
  Likewise - similarly 
  Tackle - to make a determinded effort referred to deal with problem 
  Redundant - no longer needed or useful 
  Contaminate - to make poisonous pollute 
  Steer away from/ steer clear of - avoid sth
  Asses - to evaluate

  1.	Proponent: المؤيد أو المدافع.
  	2.	Solely: فقط / بمفرده.
  	3.	Decade: عقد (فترة 10 سنوات).
  	4.	Abundant: وفير / بكثرة.
  	5.	Roughly: تقريبًا.
  	6.	Conquer: يغزو / يتغلب على.
  	7.	Vulnerable: ضعيف / معرض للخطر.
  	8.	Taxonomy: التصنيف العلمي.
  	9.	Debris: حطام / أنقاض.
  	10.	Sustainability: الاستدامة.
  	11.	Amateur: هاوٍ (غير محترف).
  	12.	Foster: يشجع / يعزز.
  	13.	Likewise: بالمثل.
  	14.	Deploy: ينشر / يستخدم.
  	15.	Tackle: يعالج / يتعامل مع.
  	16.	Redundant: زائد عن الحاجة.
  	17.	Apparently: على ما يبدو.
  	18.	Contaminate: يلوث.
  	19.	Steer away from / Steer clear of: يتجنب.
  	20.	Otherwise: خلاف ذلك.
  	21.	Assess: يقيم.
  	22.	Compile: يجمع / يُعد.
  	23.	Property: خاصية / ممتلكات.
  	24.	Generate: يولد / ينتج.
  	25.	Threat: تهديد.
  	26.	Target: هدف.
  	27.	Vigorous: قوي / نشيط.
  	28.	Guideline: إرشادات.
  	29.	By-product: منتج ثانوي.
  	30.	Promote: يروج / يعزز.
  	31.	Outbreak: تفشي / اندلاع.
  	32.	Retention: احتفاظ.
  	33.	Abide by: يلتزم بـ.
  	34.	Resilience: المرونة.
  	35.	Decline: انخفاض / يتراجع.
  	36.	Foreseeable: متوقع / يمكن التنبؤ به.
  	37.	Outline: مخطط / يلخص.
  	38.	Stem from: ينشأ عن / ينتج عن.
  	39.	A range of: مجموعة متنوعة من.
  	40.	Database: قاعدة بيانات.
  	41.	Out: خارج.
  	42.	Enormous: ضخم.
  	43.	Designate: يحدد / يعين.
  	44.	Incorporate: يدمج.
  	45.	Literate: مُتعلم / قادر على القراءة والكتابة.
  	46.	Correlate: يرتبط.
  	47.	Years to come / Generations to come: في السنوات القادمة / للأجيال القادمة.
  	48.	Congestion: ازدحام.
  	49.	Timber: خشب البناء.
  	50.	Collision: تصادم.
  	51.	Habitat: موطن طبيعي.
  	52.	Issue: قضية / مشكلة.
  	53.	Cope with: يتأقلم مع / يتعامل مع.
  	54.	Preserve: يحافظ على.

  That longer hyphen between Donor–Acceptor and then twice in structure–property–performance is called "en dash". It's used in US english to indicate a relationship and/or direction between two nouns like how a hyphen combines an adjective and noun. Like; "I have a regular 9–5," or "The Sox–Yankees rivalry is heating up this year,". In UK English though, they use them interchangeably with em dashes for parenthical inserts – especially at the ends of sentances. En dashes are probably just as rare in human content now as the em dash. Typing either of them on a physical keyboard requires using an alt-code and it isn't on the legend anywhere. Maybe the em dash is slightly more rare by virtue of it being redundant to (these).
  For some reason the spaces on either side of an em dash specifically are omitted—I'd like to know why.
  Fun Fact: The en dash is intended to be the same length on the page as an 'n' and the em dash an 'm'.

  For uni assignments I always write my own stuff… or, I mean, since AI became very capable in the last six months.. a few years ago it was all still library time and pencil highlights lol and asking a friend to proof read.... now its certainly different. I let it do the initial essay structure as a guide only.. often that will end up differently by the time the paper reaches its final draft.
  
  I double-check everything AI advices me on and I often change it a bit, as sometimes AI just missed the emphasis in a paragraph. It gets page numbers in citations wrong etc etc .. most of all in academic writing you use a very structured writing style, which AI doesn’t do well. It’s written is to complex.. I don’t have the expertise to explain this well. The first sentence in a paragraph should be giving the thesis statement; then the evidence, usually citing 2 or 3 scholars sometimes contrasting each other, then the last two or so sentences you give the paragraph a bit of body and finish with a bridge to the next paragraph.. this is also where you can criticise and reflect on the info if the essay question asks for it... anyway thats how i usually try and write my academic work... I finished my undergrad and half way through my masters... as you can probably tell in this written bit....when casually writing .. it shows I am a simple guy and English is my second language, Im sure most of you all do much better. 
  
  I let AI analyse my final draft and let it give me sentence-by-sentence advice to improve academic writing, readability, and accuracy.  But I tell it not to change my tone of voice, written style. And let it explain to me why it wants to change something… yes it takes along time on a big paper but very useful.. you actually learn something, it has changed they way I write in a small way
  
  Gee, what else… 
  
  just let AI help and coach you but write yourself. You have a writing style, especially when you get further into your studies. it is fun discovering that... I am 28 subjects in. I’m cheeky in my writing and often play with words and illustrations. Granted, my field of study is Theology so I have room for that. You might not have. I’m doing a Masters. My last two essays scored 93 percent and 89 percent. This is graduate level 9. Without AI, I was scoring 75 percent, occasionally higher, sometimes lower. So AI has helped me get better grades… slightly. 
  
  
  What it has done in a major way is decrease study and research time, tutor and coach me to be a better researcher and writer. AI readers like Speechify and Natural Reader have helped me get this far, helped process and understand difficult academic papers. Because i suck at reading long articles..  However, now with AI readers its drags me through and I get a difficult long winded academic article done in one morning... not the whole week ..... before readers.. things were bloody difficult at times. I started my undergrad 12 years ago as a part time student, working a sht job 40-50hours a week,,.. long nights in the library.. what a garbage that was... this is so much better... It is up to you all, you young ones to really takes this new tech on board and become better than we ever imagined... don't just use it as a cheat to complete your studies and party hard.....tho there is certainly  room for that :D 
   
  It’s awesome, and this is only the AI start.   Hi, I love your videos; they're informational, and your style is entertaining. I took your instructions in the video and made this prompt. I hope it will be useful:
  '''
  Objective:
  Revise the following text to make it sound as if it were written by a human, ensuring it can bypass AI detection. Your goal is to rewrite the text by eliminating common AI patterns and incorporating the nuances of natural human writing. Preserve the original meaning and core information, but transform the style, tone, and structure.
  
  Instructions:
  
  1. Rework Sentence Structure:
     * Introduce "Burstiness": Vary sentence length and structure significantly. Create a natural rhythm by mixing short, impactful sentences with longer, more complex or descriptive ones.
     * Break Repetition: Do not start sentences with the same phrases or structures repeatedly. Avoid predictable patterns like "This is...", "It is important...", "Furthermore...".
     * Use Natural Transitions: Replace formal, robotic transitions with more subtle and organic connections between ideas.
  
  2. Enhance Language and Tone:
     * Inject an Authorial Voice: Introduce a clear perspective. Add subtle critiques, nuanced stances, or personal insights where appropriate for the context.
     * Use Hedging Language: Add words and phrases that express nuance and uncertainty, such as "it seems," "perhaps," "it could be argued," "this might suggest," or "it appears to." This reflects a more cautious, human-like approach.
     * Adjust Formality: Avoid overly polished and perfect prose. The tone should be natural, which may include using a first-person voice ("I think," "I argue") or a slightly more anecdotal feel if the context allows.
  
  3. Refine Content and Word Choice:
     * Increase "Perplexity": Use less predictable word choices and phrasing. Replace generic, overused AI vocabulary.
     * Replace Vague Claims: Substitute surface-level statements and generic examples with more specific, concrete, or realistic details.
     * Avoid Predictable Patterns: Eliminate the overuse of patterns like triplets (listing three things in a row for effect).
  
  Mandatory Rules to Follow (What to Avoid):
  * DO NOT use generic AI vocabulary, including but not limited to: "delve," "robust," "innovative," "unleash," "leverage," "navigate the complexities," "in conclusion," "in the realm of," "tapestry," "showcase," "meticulous."
  * DO NOT write sentences of uniform length and rhythm.
  * DO NOT create a text that is grammatically perfect but lacks a natural flow or voice.
  * DO NOT stick rigidly to the topic without any natural, minor tangents or flow breaks that a human writer might include.
  
  Begin Revision:
  
  `[INSERT AI-GENERATED TEXT HERE]`
  '''

  Andy, I like your stuff a lot and use it regularly in class and with my faculty. One thing I have appreciated--in general--is that you aren't suggesting the use of AI as the primary tool for generating academic writing. Or are you? This post, and a couple others, feel like you are moving in that direction. There are some contradictions here, like at about 10:55-11:10 when you say inexperienced writers should take those steps to recognize better writing and become better writers. But I'd venture to guess that inexperience comes to a great degree with youth and younger scholars are much more likely to be familiar with AI tools, and perhaps also dependent upon them and thus why would they be inclined to take steps to become better academic writers? They seem to be avoiding that process de facto. I agree with you that there is a fine balance and that times are changing and expectations with them. But I wish you would talk about this part more, and more explicitly, in your videos that seem to be clickbait for "write your dissertation in 3 days" where we know damn well nobody is doing any original writing. How do we facilitate AI understanding and proper use with students when the temptation to use it indiscriminately is so high and we have videos like this that tell us how to avoid AI detectors?   🎯 Key points for quick navigation:
  
  00:05 Introduction to detecting AI writing and bypassing AI detection, with a focus on improving the naturalness of the writing.
  14:23 AI text detection relies on algorithmic cues such as perplexity (how confused the AI detector is) and burstiness (variation in structure and rhythm).
  43:58 ️ AI writing tends to have predictable sentence structures and repetitions, which makes it easy for detectors to spot.
  01:27:11 Red flags in AI writing include uniform sentence structure, lack of tangents, and overly polished language.
  03:42:01 Academic writing often lacks nuance, hedging, and personal insights, which is a key indicator of AI-generated text.
  05:31:02 AI writing often uses the "rule of three" (triplets), surface-level depth, and lacks variation in sentence structure.
  09:01:29 AI detectors can identify text as AI-generated due to surface-level writing, lack of depth, and a machine-like tone.
  10:38:44 Tips to bypass AI detection: manually improve rhythm, sentence structure, and add nuances, or use AI tools to refine the text.
  12:15:32 ️ Using a specific prompt to humanize AI-generated text can trick AI detection tools into marking it as original.
  15:04:06 Academic institutions may penalize students for writing that doesn't pass AI detection, even if it's original, due to the lack of natural variation.
  
  Made with HARPA AI

**@kaboomseo7824** (👍0 · 2025-10-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gWvgcPf3X6o&lc=Ugwor9tGSdRzaJ3w7bl4AaABAg
  - 👀 Presenter explains how to identify AI-generated writing and avoid detection.  
  - 📈 Human-like text shows higher perplexity, varied sentence length, and natural rhythm.  
  - 🚦 AI writing is marked by repetitive openings, formulaic transitions, and uniform structure.  
  - 🧽 Overly polished text without small mistakes or hedging is a strong AI indicator.  
  - 🧩 AI often produces shallow claims, predictable phrasing, triplets, and lacks personal voice.  
  - 🔬 Detectors can label AI text with high confidence, but manual or prompt-based edits can bypass them.  
  - ✅ A tailored rewrite prompt creates text that passes as 100 percent original despite AI origins.  
  - ⚠ Universities sometimes misflag genuine work, making controlled humanization strategies useful.

  Al humanization prompt:
  
  I have Al-generated text that I want to revise so it sounds like it was written by a human.
  
  Please improve it using the following guidelines:
  - Vary sentence structure and sentence length to increase burstiness
  - Introduce intellectual hesitation (e.g., "may suggest", "appears to", "is likely to")
  - Add nuance, subtle critique, or alternative perspectives where appropriate
  - Avoid overused or generic AI vocabulary like "delve," "robust," "innovative," etc.
  - Use more natural transitions (and not too many like "therefore", "moreover", "in conclusion")
  - Replace vague examples with specific, relatable, or realistic details
  - Adjust tone and style so it sounds less polished and more human (a little informal is okay)
  - If relevant, include first-person voice or a light anecdotal tone
  - Break repetition in how sentences begin (e.g., don't start every sentence with "This study..."
  - Preserve the *original meaning* and context, but improve naturalness and authenticity

  The easiest way to check for AI written content is to put the assignment prompt into ChatGPT and Grammarly, and see what comes back. If the return sounds like your student’s paper, not only did you catch AI written content being passed off as their own, but you know which software they used. I require a plagiarism agreement—because all AI writing is plagiarized from the internet—that the student signs, committing to 90% original non-AI content. I also teach them how to use Wikipedia for a topic summary and how to go to that Wikipedia article’s references (because you can’t cite a non-scholarly source like Wikipedia or Snopes), and double check that’s actually what was said so they can cite THAT reference. It’s not rocket science! It takes twice as long to rephrase AI written content than it does just to write it yourself.

  Commodity (any useful or valuable thing which you can buy or sell)
  Exploit ( To use something unfairly),
  Cultivate (develop or improve something),
  Demise (final stage/ end of life),
  Prosperity (being successful/ prosperous),
  Decade( 10 years  ),
  Alteration( change something/ Modification),
  Intermittently (at intervals/time to time/ periodically, on-of-on ),
  Extensive (covering a large area/ having a great range),
  Sophisticated (complicated/ difficult to understand),
  Diverse (various, very different, Many different parts),
  Abruptly (Suddenly, without warning)
  Result In(cause something to happen),
  Mild(not severe),
  Drastically/Dramatically/Spectacularly(Extremely, a lot, significantly)
  Tolerate (to accept),
  Threat( something that can cause serious harm, imminent threat),
  Decline( to decrease in quantity or quality, Smaller or worse),
  Coerce(force someone to do something against their will ),
  Retreat (to go away from place/person to avoid danger, Retreating shares),
  Initially ( In the beginning, at first),
  Eventually ( in the end, after alot of efforts)
  Ultimately (finally. after a series of things have happened)
  Rival (A person of thing that competes with another, a competitor)
  Data(information) 
  Conventional(usual, traditional, ordinary)
  Supersede(To replace or surpass something)
  Fossils (remains of plants and animals)
  Flourish (to grow/develop successfully)
  To thrive (to flourish/prosper/develop successfully)
  Disruption(an interruption or disturbance)
  Decay(To rot and become weaker)
  Rigid (stiff, fixed, something that can't be moved or bent)
  Preserve (to keep something from decaying or destruction)
  Depletion(the act of reducing or using something up)
  Estimate (to guess/judgement/calculate the cost, size or value of something)
  Impact(effect/influence of something on something else)
  Inhibit(to prevent or stop something from happening)
  Hibernation(type of deep sleep some animals go into during the winter/taking along nap)
  Divert(change the direction)
  Tremendous(extremely large)
  Enormous(very big)
  Emerge(to appear, to come out)
  Expand(to increase in size or scope)
  Proliferation (the act of increasing or spreading rapidly)
  Escalate(to become greater or more serious)
  Surplus(something extra/ left over)
  Eliminate (to remove/get rid of something)
  Purchase(to buy something)
  Obtain(to get something)
  Obligatory/Mandatory/Compulsory(must because of a rule or law)
  Predominant(more noticeable or important, greater in number that others)

      The text discusses phonetic conventions that make dialectal inscriptions difficult to understand. The correct word should convey obscurity or complexity.
      
      -Mephitic means "foul-smelling" and is unrelated to language or -phonetics. 
      -Autochthonous means "native" or "indigenous," which doesn’t explain why the inscriptions are hard to decipher. 
      -Recondite means "obscure" or "difficult to understand," perfectly matching the context of challenging phonetic conventions.
      -Insalubrious means "unhealthy" or "unwholesome," which is unrelated to linguistic challenges. 
      
      Correct Answer: C. Recondite.

      ​​ @laymanstrom Being a Muslim I would suggest everyone who wants to start understanding the Qur'an to just begin from reading the translation of the last 37 surahs (chapters) called the Amma para as they are small and have a heart shaking power in the words and easily understandable.
      
      Start with simple standard translation with word meaning ( app called "Al Quran tafsir and by word" )  from the last chapter- surah  Naas (surah number 114)  till surah Naba (surah number 78)
      
      Later on you can study these chapters explanation in depth by renowned lecturers ( like Dr israr  Ahmed or nouman ali khan ).
      
      Then when you have an outline and your desire to understand Quran will drive you automatically to learn Arabic language because you'd want direct communication with your creator.
      
      Keep in mind that the English translation will convey the message ..but if you want to feel the soul touching vocabulary of the Qur'an and the depth of those words, i would recommend to learn Arabic grammar (atleast)by nouman ali khan at a later stage.

  Life is replete with difficulties and setbacks. The antidote to them is to hitch your wagon to a star and then brace yourself for inevitable obstacles. The profundity of your aim compels your to move forward despite the difficulties. In this regard I'd like to share some paragraphs from a novel by Slozhenitsyn. 
  
  "What should be our attitude to difficulties?... In the sphere of the unknown, we should regard difficulties as a hidden treasure!  As a rule, the more difficult things are, the more they can help us. It is worth less if the difficulties arise from your struggle with yourself. But when they come from the increasing resistance of the object, it's splendid! 
  
  The most promising path for investigation is that on which the greatest external meets the smallest internal resistance. Setbacks must be regarded as showing the need for further application of effort and concentration of the will. If great exertions have already been made, setbacks are a still greater cause for rejoicing! They mean that our crowbar has struck the iron treasure chest! And overcoming increased difficulties is all the more valuable in that the agent grows in stature with each setback, grows in proportion to the difficulties he meets! 
  
  That doesn't mean we can never forgo further effort. Our crowbar may have struck a stone instead. Once convinced of that, or if your resources are insufficient, or in violently hostile surroundings, you may never even abandon the goal itself. But it is important to examine your reasons meticulously...
  
  Now hear the rule of the last few inches! The region of the final inches! What that means is immediately obvious in the Language of Utter Clarity. The work is nearly completed, the goal is almost attained, everything seems to have been mastered and finalized, but the quality of the thing is not quite right. Finishing touches are necessary, perhaps further research. At that moment of weariness, the temptation to abandon the work without perfecting it is particularly strong. Work in the sector of the last few inches is very, very complicated but also particularly valuable because it is carried out by the most perfect means! The rule for the last few inches amounts to just this: Do not give up work at this point! Do not put it off, or the agent's current of thought will be diverted from the region of the last few inches! And do not begrudge time spent on it, knowing that the goal is not speedy completion but the achievement of perfection. "
  
  ✨ Alexander Solzhenitsyn, In the First Circle

    ↳ **@Wordvice [channel author]** (👍0 · 2019-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1VACN6X2eF0&lc=UgwMNH4jOHn61tFC4fJ4AaABAg.8khFI3yEsks8n5cUS-Duwm
      Good question! While there isn't a perfect answer to this, one rule is to at least provide as much of your own commentary in the paper as you do paraphrasing and quoting. Moreover, there are a lot of ways to paraphrase, and sometimes you don't need to use the words or data of another researcher to make your overall point, even when you are using the basic (or even specific) conclusions of that researcher. In addition, you should always read through articles of the journal/conference/publication to which you are submitting to see what other researchers do. This can help determine how many sources to include in your literature review and how much reference to previous work should be quoted or paraphrased.

If you have a vocabulary diary or note app, you can take a few minutes every few hours to go through your phrases.     ↳ **@highlevellistening [channel author]** (👍68 · 2025-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=I-DiPTWUxyg&lc=Ugymii_VPOTiYqnbbGV4AaABAg.ABO2CNWCfAGABR9zkJG9H5
      Thanks so much for your kind message! It's actually a very common issue - most people can understand a lot of words in a 2nd language, but struggle with speaking. 
      
      It's usually because when you are a student, you listen and read *a lot*. Teachers talk to you, there are podcasts, audiobooks, YouTube videos and grammar textbooks etc etc. 
      
      This is important useful, but this method is only training your "receptive" skills. Speaking, however, is a "productive" skill. The only way to improve a productive skill is to produce! My own method is to take a single sentence (with a structure or word I really want to remember) and repeat it and repeat it and repeat it and repeat. And also write it and write it and write it and write it again and again until it comes out quickly and naturally. I take a break (of 1 or 2 days), then do it again. After some time, it does start to "stick" and I can produce it quickly and under a bit of pressure (someone looking at me!). It sounds quite old school, but it works for me. It's really still the best way to practice productive skills, especially if you don't have a native speaker or a partner to practice with often.
      
      I hope some of that helps!

  Excellent video! What's the difference between touch base and check in exactly? They seem pretty much the same
    ↳ **@highlevellistening [channel author]** (👍0 · 2026-07-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=I-DiPTWUxyg&lc=UgwpfIhg_pYU-Z9T7OJ4AaABAg.AZ2luUqwr2YAZ2tQxylcdJ
      That's a good question, and they’re very close!
      
      Touch base = make quick contact, usually about a specific topic.
      Example: “Let’s touch base about the meeting.”
      
      Check in = ask for an update or see how someone/something is doing.
      Example: “I’m checking in to see how the project is going.”
      
      So in business, they often overlap, but touch base sounds more like a quick connection, while check in can feel a bit more about progress or wellbeing. Hope that makes sense!

  Just like in music, when simplicity dominates, complexity becomes expected. When repetition takes over, we begin to crave randomness. And when randomness persists, people start looking for familiarity—or at least a pattern. Sameness naturally creates a hunger for variation. The notable asymmetry is this: while sameness demands change, variation never wears out its welcome. It’s a one-way relationship—people may tire of the predictable, but never of the unexpected.

      The notion that complexity is preferable to simplicity is the result of a limited, over-simplified understanding of culture and the human nature that drives it. Taste norms in art, especially in architecture and the culinary world, tend to follow a cyclical pattern oscillating between simplicity and complexity. The endless complexity of contrived creations overwhelm us. It’s why we craved for minimalist elegance after the excesses of the art deco movement. It’s why haute cuisine evolved to focus on two–three flavors maximum and flavor-maxxing is discouraged.
      
      Unpredictability isn’t so hot either. Turns out that variation does wear out its welcome. The anxiety of uncertainty exhausts us. It’s why people “settle down” to lead a quiet life after adventuring in their youth. It’s why the comfort zone exists.

  To start with, this video helped me revise essentials of writing. The first essential I revised concerned transitions. By employing transitions in the form of words and phrases — such as more importantly, by extension, and for comparison — I can leave clues to guide the reader through my writing. In addition, I revised why varying the length and structure of sentences plays an important part in my writing. For instance, I should use complex compound sentences that contain subordinate clauses so that the reader can glide through my writing on a ramp as opposed to taking one step at a time on a staircase. Coming to modifications, every writer should have this tool in their inventory as well. In simple terms, modifications refer to converting nouns into past participles, but there are limitless other forms of modifications, making it hard to mention each one. More importantly, variety and contrast are vital to maintain flow. I not only have to mix the aforementioned techniques up but also at times employ only some in one paragraph just to use altogether new ones in the another to generate variety and contrast in my writing respectively. In any case, I pray that those who have made this far reading my reply succeed in their aims of transforming their writing

  What is a "philospher's stone" in 8:30 might I ask? I coudn't search it up.
  
  Recently, while doing re-reading of my own essays, I've realizied there were a lots of clichés (that I didn't know they were) transitionings/subordinatings that I uses too often to the point it becomes my own signature. Your metaphor of the stair and the ramp gave me an interesting idea: By intentionally inserting a segment of the 'full steps' into the rather overall smooth 'ramp', it will helps creating an uncanniness, a sudden yet subtle change in the narration of the writing that give readers a hint that something has happened in their own reading voice, without telling them. It would feel like you were gliding in your car on a perfectly smooth road and felt a small bump that make you wonder if it was a pot hole or was it something else?
  
  Maybe there were already a name for this technique that could also convey subtle but important changes and messages. Though, to be able to do the "show, don't tell" in a medium where you need to l tell yourself, I think that's pretty cool.
  
  Also finding your channel among the mass AI and rage-baiting youtube algorithm is like digging your own grave and strucking gold

  I really love the examples at 05:58 about starting the sentences with "Because, If, Although" etc. but in my native language (Turkish) it is incorrect to start a sentence with those words since they are conjunctions, they are there to connect the sentences; meaning they have to be between at least two sentences. 
  I also hate how in Turkish, it is also incorrect to use a comma before and after conjunctions. (The reason they give you is any conjunction you use already treats the sentence like a comma is there, you stop for .5 secs, if you would put a comma before or after a conjunction, it would make it like the sentence is over blah blah blah)
  You probably won't believe me but I once cried because of this genius (!) rule. A sentence sounds exactly how I want if I put a comma after an "and" for example, but Turkish doesn't allow it since it apparently already counts the conjunctions as a semi-stop. Good thing there is no such rule in English.

  Andrew, as an engineer, I take umbrage, albeit only slightly, with your analogy of steps and inclines. If you want to pander to the analytically inclined amongst your listeners, perhaps a more robust analogy would to envision the transition of the paragraph in terms of "how steep" is the ascent/descent of the material covered. The steeper the incline, the greater the need for steps. Of course, transitioning between in a sufficiently complex paragraph goes without saying. Just sayin'.
  
  As I'm new to your channel, I may be asking an old question with a cogent answer already published by you. Still, I'll put it out there, then go looking around. When we're talking writing flow as in relates to sentence structure, what role does the spoken word play in crafting sentences intended for a reading audience? I've pondered this question for some time now, thinking about the career of Samuel Clemens. While he earned his chops as a newspaper writer, his success as a humorist and author contemporary fiction hinged largely upon a phenomena of the day that is still part of pretty much a part of our everyday culture but which we tend to overlook as to its importance. When 19th century and early 20th century authors went on a "book tour" it was not a simply affair where they sat at a table and autograph copies of their latest work. Rather, they held readings to as large an audience as they could gather in whatever town they found themselves. After which they'd engage in a bit commerce with those whom they'd won over with the reading. What we likely overlook today is that interactive quality to those readings and how they help shape the structure of the written word for those authors with a keen eye and ear. It wasn't enough to be able to speak the characters' vernaculars and lend them each a unique voice, both in sound and quality. Rather, the story had to flow from one sentence to the next, as the speaker spoke the story. If an author could not convince his or her listeners that a story was worth hearing, then how might he or she convince them to part with coin to finish reading it?
  
  While authors now have the means to reach much larger audiences, from all around the globe, and even present their works in audio and video formats, sans the need for an angel patron to get the work out into public, how does a modern day writer acquire that very crucial listener feedback from potential readers to tell him whether he has struck upon the secret sauce of story telling that might make him the next Mark Twain? Some writers have the good fortune of family and friends who can be both tolerant and keenly critical, but I fear that may be more an exception than rule. How can an aspiring writer capture what Clemens and his contemporaries found themselves immerse in out of necessity? Or, is the path to writing no longer integral to the process and forever lost?
  
  If you got this far, thanks for letting me ramble. I remember that infamous phrase repeated by my tenth grade English teacher, each time I walked into class, "Angels, if you don't want the world to know just how smart you really are, then don't every show them your first draft." While I haven't a clue why she was always looking at me when she said it, I hope I cleaned this up so that it reads good.
  
  Keep up the good work.

  Question: What do you think about words that are very present in academic papers, such as: moreover, however, so on and so forth? I am reading a book about stylish writing and the writer argues that great writers can write great paragraphs without using too big an amount of linking words.
  Do you think that great writers can creat great academic papers without these ‘basic’ linking words?
    ↳ **@WritingwithAndrew [channel author]** (👍2 · 2021-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hhVic18H4u4&lc=Ugy5bKAD5fclUbF-IHp4AaABAg.9QBn__GYRPM9QBqaljAEqZ
      Interesting question. Most style commentators are usually guided by the standards of literary writing (especially fiction), so they make strong statements that don't work in every situation. Those kinds of transitions would probably look odd in a novel, but they can be really useful in academic writing for giving readers a sense of how abstract ideas are related to each other. In literary writing there are other tools (like chronological narration) to help readers find their way, so overt transitions like that may seem a little heavy-handed. It's definitely possible that academic writers could do without them, but academic writers are also doing a very different job that requires different tools (so I'd hesitate to outlaw them in all cases)

      @WritingwithAndrew  *How To Make Sticky Sentences Flow*
      
      True; my writing style since has doubled back to sort of using sticky sentences/glue words (almost like a full circle) and I can honestly say it's refreshing to just go back to my normal style of writing, now enhanced with the power of grammar structure; punctuation and all. I don't think I'll be switching out of this style for another, as it plays to phrases where I like a melodical tone; it feels unrestrained and untempered, and I freakin' love the sound and flow of it.
      Why stop, right? 
      As rigid as we temper our writing to be like everybody else's or follow those magical “rules” of writing, the truth is it comes down to your own level of writing and what you're comfortable with; I know I like my style, as it appeals to what I like to read and write, and I won't have others tell me that isn't right; I write my own rules, and no one can tell you that's how you do it. The best we can hope for is an answer: but the best of dreams we make from our creativity pours out of the way we do things best.
      And that, my philoscribophile, is how we learn to mold our own writing into its shape. And the best of times, even at the worst of times, comes out of what we make. Imagination, and...creativity.

  One of the best ways to build sophisticated vocabulary is to listen to radio talk show hosts, who have studied history, politics, or law.   So, back in high school, our 9th grade English teacher gave my class an activity to choose and write vocabulary words and their definitions on the board to share with everyone each week. We all took turns via a hat that chose the student at random.
  
  For context, I was previously homeschooled and deeply sheltered. 9th grade was my first public school experience ever. And I, having only heard the word from classic literature like Wuthering Heights, decided it would be a fantastic idea to walk up to the white board and write "ejaculate" on it with the definition that essentially means "exclaimed or said with verve" in total naive 14 year old seriousness.
  
  You can imagine the reaction from my classmates that followed and my complete and utter confusion over why everyone was snickering at what I thought was a really cool if not archaic word. 🤦🏼‍♀️
    ↳ **@KimberlyChapman** (👍178 · 2026-07-22) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pFmGw8im3bI&lc=UgyWPsYsQttYW1zKUXl4AaABAg.AZDV5gWnE-tAZGabz8fNoN
      I wasn’t homeschooled but I grew up in a very sheltered, prudish household. In seventh grade we were to select our own words to learn to spell every week and by the end of the week, submit a paragraph using the words. I liked to pick mine at random by flipping the dictionary to a random page and plonking down my index finger. If i didnt know the word it landed upon, I chose it.
      
      One week I chose a word in the m section, the definition of which was “self-excitement”. I can’t say it in a comment here but let’s just say it was…masterful. Perhaps baiting.
      
      I didn’t know it. I swear. 
      
      I presented my list to the teacher for approval and he glared at me and asked, “Really?”  I must’ve looked genuinely innocent, because I was, and I think he didn’t want to say anything that would land him in trouble. 
      
      So I learned to spell it and the other words, submitted a paragraph that included something about someone doing something they found exciting, but all very innocent and wholesome.
      
      It was many years later when I learned what the word really means. 
      
      I wish I could go back and apologise to that poor teacher!

      Still I find this puzzling about English literature. I recently listened to a Lord of the Rings audiobook and it was just so jarring how Tolkien's rich and varied vocabulary contrasted with the omnipresent "said" at the end of ever second line of dialogue, including questions. I just wonder where this trend even came from, because it's definitely not the norm in Europe: in fact, I don't think any other European language would tolerate this level of repetition. Hyperbole has to be used sparingly, or it gets silly and breaks the immersion.  Metaphors are fine, unless very overused,  and non-literal illustrative language usually  doesn't work without  a lot of context.  For people needing advice on it, its unlikely to go well.

**@uttonio** (👍14 · 2021-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=E_GSkiaMnx4&lc=UgzhWEIogg3lT4KH_yh4AaABAg
  I already know ameliorate and mitigate so...
  
  1. reticent (adj): unwilling to speak about one's thoughts and feelings.
  The students remain reticent when it comes to answering the teacher's question.
  
  2. pragmatic (adj): solving the problem in a way that is based on the reality rather than fixed ideas or theories, taking realistic approach.
  ~ His decision to study Computer Science is a pragmatic one.
  
  3. equivocal (adj): 
  - of words or statement: beating around the bush, being deliberately vague in meaning.
  ~ She gave an equivocal answer, which is typical of a politician.
  
  - of action or behavior: difficult to understand explain clearly or easily.
  ~ The research produced equivocal results, giving scientists a hard time to analyze the findings.
  
  4. ephemeral (adj): lasting for a very short time.
  ~ In this musical world, one artist's fame is usually ephemeral.

      Hello, Chinese student. This sentence you posted is good, but I will help you make it a little better. Here is what I would do with it:
      "Thank you Veronika. I am a Chinese student, and I have been struggling in my learning of English for a period of time. It is so great to meet you." 
      Since "Thank you Veronica." is a complete thought, I replaced the comma mark with a period mark. A period is used at the end of a sentence, and usually, a sentence is a complete thought or statement. In the second sentence, I added the word, "and" which connects a second idea to the first idea, and it is often used after a comma mark. A comma mark indicates a brief pause in the thought that is being communicated. I also added some helping words which are how English is normally structured. The last sentence is a complete thought, and I started it with a "capital" letter. A capital letter is a larger version of a small letter, although they do not always have the same form. The good news for you is that English only uses 26 letters, and not 3,000 pictograms. I wish you well in your language journey.

  NOTES TO MYSELF: 1. Use compound sentences: combination of basic sentences:  means sentences with two or more subjects. Connect with but, yet, nor, because, for, or. 2. More Relative Clauses: defining/non-defining : who whose that which where when. Climate change, which has been an issue for many decades, will.. _ non-defining güzel ve kullanması uydurabilmesi yaratabilmesi güzzel. 3. Inversion: Grammer area? Dozens of .. By … + ing. By taking but also .. not only can we … değş tokuş 4. Cleft sentence: It is education, that needs more investment. (More investment should be done in the education area demek yerine). 5. Passive voice: It is believed that climate change.. (Scientists believe that demek yerine) 6. Cohesive devices: Howeverr, Nevertheless, Moreover, Furthermore, In contrast. FLOW IS THE KEY. FLOW IS THE GOAL. THANK YOU VERY MUCH BEN TEACHER!! 🎉❤

      English Conversation topic: Dining Out with Friends
      
      1. Planning to Dine Out:
      
      "Hey, do you want to grab dinner together this weekend?"
      "I'm craving [type of cuisine]. Would you be interested in trying that restaurant with me?"
      "Let's go out for dinner to celebrate [occasion]."
      "I heard about this new restaurant downtown. Do you want to check it out with me?"
      "I'm in the mood for some good food and company. Who's up for dinner tonight?"
      
      2. Making Plans:
      
      "Sounds like a plan! What time should we meet?"
      "Count me in! Where are we meeting?"
      "I'm down for dinner. Which restaurant did you have in mind?"
      "I'm free after 7 PM. Does that work for everyone?"
      "Great! Let's make a reservation to avoid waiting too long."
      
      3. Choosing a Restaurant:
      
      "Do you have any preferences for cuisine, or are you open to suggestions?"
      "I'm in the mood for Italian food. How does that sound?"
      "Is there a particular restaurant you've been wanting to try?"
      "I know a great sushi place nearby. Would you be interested?"
      "Let's find a place that accommodates everyone's dietary preferences."
      
      4. Ordering Food:
      
      "I think I'll start with the [appetizer]. What about you?"
      "Everything on the menu looks delicious. I'm having a hard time deciding!"
      "I'm going to try the [dish]. Has anyone had it before?"
      "I'm allergic to [ingredient], so I'll need to make sure it's not in my dish."
      "Let's share some dishes family-style so we can try a little bit of everything."
      
      5. Enjoying the Meal:
      
      "This [dish] is amazing! I'm glad I ordered it."
      "I've never tried [ingredient] before. It's actually really good!"
      "The presentation of these dishes is so impressive."
      "The flavors in this dish are so well-balanced."
      "I'm really enjoying the atmosphere of this restaurant."
      
      6. Conversation Topics:
      
      "So, what's everyone been up to lately?"
      "Have you seen any good movies or TV shows recently?"
      "Did anyone hear about [current event]? What are your thoughts on it?"
      "Let's reminisce about some of our favorite memories together."
      "What are your plans for the upcoming [holiday or special occasion]?"
      
      7. Paying the Bill:
      
      "Should we split the bill evenly, or does anyone want to pay separately?"
      "I'll take care of the tip. Does anyone have cash?"
      "Let me get this one. You can treat next time."
      "Are we ready for the bill, or would anyone like dessert or another drink?"
      "Thanks for joining me for dinner, everyone. It's my treat this time."

  _affect (v): to influence, to have an impact on sth
  _effect (n): the result of an influence
  _affect (v): to influence sth
  _affect (n): (the affect something)
  _effect (n): (to have an effect on something)
  _accept: to agree to take sth from someone/to say yes to an offer or an invitation
  _except: but not
  _sight: the ability to see
  _cite: to speak/to write words taken from somebody eles
  _site: the location or place of aomething
  _advice (n): somebody's opinion that can help you (to give advice to someone/to ask for advice)
  _advise (v): to give a somebody advice
  _eminent: famous, well-known
  _imminent: likely to happen soon, there is the possibility of it happening any moment now
  _immanent: inherent, intrinsic, sth that you naturally have

**@improveyourenglishlearning7872** (👍249 · 2023-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gHmMWBpUzgc&lc=Ugz7JSMHU5DQFD89FrB4AaABAg
  Advanced collocations
  1) "To Wholeheartedly agree"
  (To completely and enthusiastically agree)
  2) "To respectfully disagree"
  3) "To forge relationships"
  (To make an effort to create strong connection/bond with someone)
  4) "To extol virtues"
  (To praise positive qualities)
  5) "To be extricably linked"
  (things which cannot be separated, which have an essential connection)
  6) "To render speechless"
  (To surprise someone so that they can't speak anything)
  7) "To scupper a plan"
  (To cause a plan to fail)
  8) "Scathing attack"
  (Very critical or unkind verbal attack)
  9) "Blissfully unaware"
  (Not knowing something unpleasant)
  10) "Rekindle the passion/love"
  (To have strong, positive feelings for someone/something again)

  Collocations are an essential part of mastering English, and it's highly likely they make communication more natural. I wholeheartedly agree with the idea that learning them is crucial for fluency, though I can imagine some might vehemently disagree about their importance compared to grammar rules. Even if we respectfully disagree, we can still forge relationships with others through shared learning experiences. Collocations are inextricably linked to sounding fluent, and their elegance can render speechless those who hear them used effectively. Neglecting them could scupper plans for advanced language skills. While some critiques of collocations can feel like a scathing attack, I think many are blissfully unaware of how impactful they are. Videos like this can truly rekindle passion for learning and extol the virtues of collocations as a vital tool in any language learner’s journey!

  Let me mention, these expressions mostly exist in other languages: I speak Hungarian so it is easy to understand these collocations. F.e. "scupper" in Hungarian in a mirror translation is: to sink a ship by hitting a hole into the side, so it will sink sooner or later. I think collocation is frequently used in newspapers for the sake of better understanding and to spare a lot of work for journalists. But the use of collocations can be applied in high literature when the writer's opinion is somehow sarcastic about the state of the world or people. Just think about Bertold Brecht.

  Proper Collocations are a bit more complex. They have to be the ONLY combination in a group of words. ONLY. So 'fish and chips', 'bucket and spade' , 'Happy New Year', for example, are collocations. 'Merry Xmas' isn't because we also say 'Happy Xmas', but 'Happy Birthday' is a collocation.

  Hi teacher! I've a question. Blissfully unaware is a synonyn of "oblivious to"? Thank you!
    ↳ **@cyruschang1904** (👍0 · 2023-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gHmMWBpUzgc&lc=Ugx6AX9n6VUo0zGOD9F4AaABAg.9fqnH0UCNRe9frPxaQzia9
      -to be oblivious to/of something means to be unaware of or not to be concerned about what is happening around oneself.
      -to be unaware of something cannot be used to mean "not to be concerned about something"
      -We use to be blissfully unaware of to mean not to be aware of something unpleasant/upsetting only. It is correct to say "he is unaware of the good/bad news", but we would only say "he is blissfully unaware of the bad news", never "he is blissfully unaware of the good news".
    ↳ **@tothepointenglishwithben. [channel author]** (👍0 · 2023-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gHmMWBpUzgc&lc=Ugx6AX9n6VUo0zGOD9F4AaABAg.9fqnH0UCNRe9fsAyaJ3Ehr
      They can be synonymous in many contexts but, as Cyrus mentioned, "oblivious to" often has the  connotation of being indifferent.

  Could I use "blissfully unaware" in a negative sense, such as: Today marked the 21st anniversary of 9/11, but most media outlets were blissfully unaware.?
    ↳ **@tothepointenglishwithben. [channel author]** (👍1 · 2023-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gHmMWBpUzgc&lc=UgxlBIuXANFgH5KB7ch4AaABAg.9fqgvqrrkHc9fqmeXpfbtc

    ↳ **@cyruschang1904** (👍1 · 2023-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gHmMWBpUzgc&lc=UgxlBIuXANFgH5KB7ch4AaABAg.9fqgvqrrkHc9frC_YoRWma
      We always say to be blissfully unaware/ignorant of something unpleasant, never of something nice. For example, we would never say "Ben is blissfully unaware of the good news". We are always upset about something bad, so if we are unaware of it, we would remain blissful (happy).

In addition to being the most disconnected from reality and boring language-learning activity one can engage in, spaced repetition/flashcard learning of vocabulary results in a superficial, poor-quality kind of “learning”. Creating and practicing flashcards can feel reassuring because it gives the illusion of having an organized way of “catching” those thousands of slippery eels of unknown words and expressions in a new language, but one is far better off if one resists the temptation and boring waste of time.       I've been using it for about ten years as well, and I agree. I just have way to many examples and tangible benefits from using it. It somehow makes the whole process feel less daunting and I very consistently see my recall of vocabulary from the Anki deck translate into my ability to recognize it in the wild. I don't know how I would even continue learning without it.
      
      This idea of having too many reviews or spending too much time with Anki isn't a problem with the method--it's how you use it. If you add too many cards to learn each day, your reviews will pile up. In my case, I've been using one particular deck for about seven months and only have about 45 reviews every day. I can knock it out in about 20 minutes with my new cards. It's very easy to get too ambitious but you have to be patient and think long-term or you will burn yourself out with 200 reviews. The point is going to be to focus on your reviews, not the new cards. It's probably best to do 10 or less cards a day, which doesn't seem like a lot but every day you're going to be reviewing a lot of material, which is the whole point as opposed to the arbitrary number of new cards you choose to appear every day.

**@zeljkothegreekserb** (👍49 · 2023-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tCBbGbRvkGo&lc=UgzLQnNirzxcBrXtWFN4AaABAg
  I used Anki wrongly before (word to word cards or premade sentences by others) and barely learned 1/3 of the words, I gave up afterwards, but I tried again and once I 1. started creating MY own sentences (for encoding purposes), 2. with the target word being written in the native language and the answer being in the foreign one (to evade the false-knowledge trap of knowing what a "bicicleta" is, even though I'd never remember it going from English to Spanish) and 3. creating a new sentence and thus more context whenever I forget something, I have come to the point where I can easily learn over 50 words a day even if I don't put much effort in, with only <5 spaced repetitions until I can comfortably and actively remember the word for months and even years. By comparison, on Memrise or using premade Anki decks, I often had cards I repeated over 30, 40 times and never learned in the end, so does creating my own optimized cards take a lot of time? It does, in fact majority of my time is spent creating cards, but if those cards can afterwards be learned with minimal repetitions, instead of wasting 10 times more time reviewing the same cards over and over and over, then I wouldn't say it is a waste of learning time, but the exact opposite, the best possible learning time-investment I can make. Anki is an amazing tool if it used in such an optimized way, but that is just what it is, a tool, same as how a book is a tool, even Assimil itself is a tool, but a tool can be used effectively or it can cause more pain than gain if used incorrectly.

**@Tenahio** (👍22 · 2023-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tCBbGbRvkGo&lc=UgwrOm68KnRv9pdlWSN4AaABAg
  I agree that Anki can be difficult to use in a smart way. Almost all my Anki cards are key phrases from texts which I listen to many times so that I get both passive exposure and can retrieve useful parts, while remembering the context. It's true that the cards in a deck tend to pile up if you miss reviewing for some time, but the neat thing with Anki is that it takes into account the time you didn't review, so if you review a card a year after it was due, and you remember it, the intervals will increase automatically. I was taking up Spanish again recently after years not using it actively, had 800 cards on Spanish in Anki, which took 3 hours to review, but I remembered almost 500 of those and won't need to review those again for a long time, and the 300 or so which I failed are much easier to remember again than fresh cards and their intervals increase much more rapidly.

**@rashidah9307** (👍7 · 2023-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tCBbGbRvkGo&lc=UgzBZ04X5_84MA7ihA14AaABAg
  Luca, you decided to stir up the pot with this video! Lol. I've been using Anki for 2+ years, and I think most of your critiques can be avoided or at least mitigated (but not, of course, for everyone). Getting started on the phone app was super easy for me. I never understand when people complain about it being complicated to get started with Anki, and I'm not particularly tech savvy. I always take my cards from context (such as sentences that my tutor wrote down for me in Skype that I cut and paste), I almost never use single words, and I think it's pretty easy to understand the algorithm and not overwhelm yourself with too big of a deck. I only add about 15 cards per week, which doesn't take a huge chunk of time. I know my limits! Lol. I've heard it said by Scott Young, I believe, that the process of creating flashcards IS studying. It's not a waste of time. I'm reviewing my notes from my lesson or a reading passage when I'm adding cards, and I am typing in a different alphabet--all good things to practice. But, most importantly, once I've created that flashcard, it is stored in the most convenient place for me, which is on my phone. I can review my flashcards anywhere, even on a busy day when I don't have time to sit down to study anything. I believe the biggest drawback of the bidirectional approach is that I need to have time to sit down and study every day. . . which is not the reality of my life right now with a husband, teenager, pets, and multiple professional hats. So, for me, the convenience, the way Anki organizes my study time for me, and the ability to actually get it done are the reasons why I've stuck with it. And it works for me.
