**@andrzejkulinski1886** (👍3 · 2023-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tCBbGbRvkGo&lc=Ugyr18I6EioSWdXWU-t4AaABAg
  High Luca, 
  it's probably the first time I disagree with what you say to some extent, so I would like to pinpoint some advantages of Anki that give it some edge over other tools and techniques.
  I started my journey with Swedish using bidirectional translation method. Unfortunately, I didn't balance it out with enough listening and ended up with developing fake prosody (which in turn harmed my listening abilities and led to a funny situation. Being on holidays in Sweden I was able to speak quite freely without any prior speaking practice, but couldn't understand what people were saying back).
   I managed to "heal" it with doing microdictations with anki - on the front card I put an audio sentence from a TV series I was currently watching. The task was to write it down. 3 months of 2 new cards a day burnt the right prosody into my brain. 
  Also, it can work well to augment your biderectional translation method - you can create a flashcard type where you need to translate from your L1 to L2 or vice versa, but you can add L2 audio to the L2 side so as not to develop fake prosody.
  What is more, I see benefits of anki for the category of learners who have a tendency to rely too much on reading and distort the original sounds of a given language (i'm one of these people). You can create a deck where on the front side you have only audio in L2, on the backside only a definition/translation in L1. This way you bypass reading and teach your brain to rely on aural stimulus more. Such a deck would be used at the very first stage of learning a new language. Of course, the drawback is that it would have to be pre-made by another person.
  These are my two cents or more. Hope it was worth reading for you and other subscribers.
  Regards!

**@PeronJames** (👍41 · 2024-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tCBbGbRvkGo&lc=UgzO8V38245oM8lqS5B4AaABAg
  4 out of 5 of your problems are completely irrelevant if you're actually using anki effectively.
  
  1. With popup dictionaries you can have 1 click cards with meaning and pronunciation, and 2 click cards that also add the context sentence, audio and image
  2. It's true that it can become addicting, that's why it's important to not add every single new word you see, but only add those that are important/common enough or relevant to you. Just use common sense and frequency dictionaries.
  3. If you enable hiding leeches this pretty much goes away. If a card becomes a chore it automatically hides itself and you can add it again the next time you see it in context (if you want). If for some reason reviews are getting too much for you, you can simply turn off new cards for a couple days and get that number down.
  4. This would be true, except that the most effective method of using anki is sentence mining. Like I mentioned above, you can literally have an anki card with all the context you found it in (sentence, audio and image) in two clicks, without even needing to pause the video.

  Petunia Teyze muazzam oğluna sisli gözlerle baktı

**@fellowsidiomas** (👍1 · 2023-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tCBbGbRvkGo&lc=UgyV_Kk5zgeCeCspGQd4AaABAg
  How to use SRS effectively:
  1.TAKE A SHORT PIECE O CONTENT
  2.LEARN IT DEEPLY.
  3. REVIEW IT IN A VARIETY OF WAYS (OVER THE COURSE OS A SINGLE WEEK).
  
  DAY 1: READ the content and listen to the audio file, using the translation in my mother tongue to try to understand the text as deeply as possible.
  DAY 2: ANALYZE the phonetic patterns of the text: -pronunciation, -intonation, -word stress.
  DAY 3: REVIEW the content in a brand-new way: -listening to the audio, -reading the text, -or something else entirely!
  DAY 4: MAKE A PERSONALIZED translation of the text in my native language.
  DAY 5: TAKE my native translation from the previous day, and try to verbally translate it back into my target language.
  DAY 6: TAKE my native-language translation and re-translating it in writing back into the original language. Then, I make note of any errors, forgotten words, or mistranslations.

**@OmniKoneko** (👍12 · 2023-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tCBbGbRvkGo&lc=Ugy27A0V5tq1ZV8yLsV4AaABAg
  All of your points go void once you think about it for even a second, since they can be solved through self awareness, different decisions or by changing the settings.
  
  1. Making flash cards don't waste learning time because it gives you more time with the language within an activity. It allows you to sentence mine on your own which gives you autonomy in the language. As well you don't have to make your own cards, there are plenty of good community made decks you can download and modify specific cards that you want to be different.
  
  2. Anything can become an addiction, all you have to do is be self aware of what you're doing like with anything like eating candy for example, you wouldn't say to someone that they shouldn't eat candy because there's a possiblity to become addicted, you would tell them to eat it in moderation and have other food that offloads the negative parts of eating said candy. Also it's funny how in the first point you said that using anki is bad because it takes so much time then you say that it's easy for it to become an addiction because it's so easy to create cards through your phone and such... You can't just pick and choose.
  
  3. Reviewing old cards can be a chore, but just because it's a hard thing or annoying thing to do, doesn't mean it's bad for you or that you shouldn't do it, plenty of people work at jobs they don't like but they gain lots of great benefits at the end like going on vacation, doing activities with friends, having a place to sleep, etc. I'm sure most people especially beginners would say that learning a langauge in general is a chore, so if it already is then why not choose the way that gives them progress the fastest.
  
  4. Flashcards take context out of language, not true, because if you looked at how people utilize Anki and the creation of cards then you would know that it's not true and you even touch a bit on it with how people create cards from shows and people also have screenshots/videos that play along with their cards. Also through sentence mining instead of just learning straight vocabulary you'll gain the context, plenty of people learn vocabulary through this way and you can highlight specific words in a sentence when creating cards so you know which one you're learning. And again there are plenty of pre-made decks you can use to save time or services to use to automatically create cards from a scene of a show with one click of a button.
  
  You said that your method is better but I would argue that it's much easier, faster and more convient to be able to go straight to your deck where you are on your phone, computer, tablet, etc. and be able to study and see the number of reviews/new-cards go down in comparison to learning phrases deeply, learning all of the intonation/pronunciation/word-stress, and translate it a hundred different ways while in your example "having a family to take care of". And it's especially not beginner friendly because most people would agree that when starting a new skill they want to ease into it not learn all of this very academic parts of a language. 
  
  You should not be pushing people to use or not use a particular way of learning, the most important thing for anyone is for them to spend time with the language and make progress, if a person has a way they enjoy doing it then that's the most important thing they should do becuase it will keep them interested in the language and not give up.

**@brianpenttila5511** (👍2 · 2024-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tCBbGbRvkGo&lc=UgyaAojczdL_-i0trGh4AaABAg
  It sounds like you have some good thoughts about language learning. That's great, but your criticisms of Anki seem quite exaggerated. 1) it doesn't take minutes to create a card, 2) you can apply context to any vocabulary word through using simple sentences (your example of different meanings of "light" are easily overcome this way), 3) as concepts are memorized, the frequency of review "burden" lessens; of course if you are learning thousands of words and phrases you may find this a burden, but you can remove review of cards very easily as they become unnecessary (assuming you are exposed through regular reading, listening and speaking in the new language), 4) in your method, more context means more time/effort and likely with diminishing returns. I don't know how you can confidently say that Anki doesn't work "for the majority of learners." Given it's widespread popularity, I would say that clearly it does work. And I don't think anyone suggests that Anki ALONE can make you a fluent speaker; it's just a tool, and a very useful one for me.

**@jeremybuckets** (👍1 · 2024-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tCBbGbRvkGo&lc=Ugzf4uRRZlJw4IrXQZt4AaABAg
  IMO Anki is best for 1. brand new learners, to bootstrap their vocabulary with the most commonly used words in a language 2. advanced learners, to learn phrases and idioms that don't show up frequently but are important for enriching vocabulary and understanding. In the former case, if the language is remotely popular there is already a high quality 1k word deck for it so the initial effort is zero. In the latter case, you have enough of a scaffolding of the language that you really don't need much to the card—a sentence that puts the phrase in context and the meaning on the back. You're at the stage where you don't need pictures or audio files for every single thing, you just need some text to prompt your brain to make connections to related things it already knows. Those cards take mere seconds to create.
  
  Where people get stuck is trying to learn every single individual word they come across in the intermediate stage. You need a passive vocabulary of something like 40,000 words to reach native-level comprehension. Learning this via flashcards would take decades—it's literally just too inefficient and too much work. The only way to achieve this is mass consumption of native media. Stick to using flash cards as a tool to learn complex phrases that stick out as being important to you, and rely on lots and lots of immersion to fill in the gaps.

**@petrosstefanidis6396** (👍13 · 2023-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tCBbGbRvkGo&lc=Ugz_KQQgDBNHLRjZyTl4AaABAg
  Solid critique. I should say thought that after 3 years of using it (in 4 languages including my native language!) it's still working like a charm😄
  
  1. It's true that it consumes time to learn how to use and it's labourious to make the cards themselves, let aside reviewing them. That is indeed something to keep in mind. As you said in a previous video, it's useful to review how much time you spend on each language learning activity compared to how much it helps you learn and time spent on Anki should indeed be limited to the minimum. Those are problems you deal with in the beginning though. After a certain amount of time you just become "fluent" in using the app and everything is almost effortless.
  
  2. It can be addictive, absolutely. I've been there and it's important to not make a habit of stopping every couple of minutes to add another new world. That can ruin the experience of both reading and using Anki. Personally I ended up using it when it feels important and compelling to learn an unknown word.
  
  3. Missing a day can be a pain in the ass. The most important thing to remember here though, is that the amount of cards depends solely on your input! If it feels like too much, just reduce the amount you add. If you want to set targets, challenge yourself and plough on, add more. Simple as that. It doesn't have to be always the same amount of input. For example, despite of having hundreds upon hundreds of cards in Spanish, at this point I only get 10-12 cards per day to review. That's 4-5 minutes. The more time passes, the bigger the interims become and the less time you have to spend. A lot of times though I feel myself it would be great to be able to pause the app (when I'm sick for example). 
  
  4. It always makes sense for me to use Anki as a tool in combination with whatever else I'm doing to learn. So I don't just download random decks to learn. On the contrary I add new cards with context that I find interesting and compelling while reading, listening to music or watching a video or a movie. This way there's a good - imo -  balance between focusing on the world/phrase and context. 
  
  5. Sounds interesting. Why not combine it with Anki thought? Could be fun 😊
  
  Keep it up Lucca! Pretty good video even if we disagree.

  Interesting video. However, I don't agree with you. E.g. the process of preparing a flashcard is already part of learning. The words are not totally of of context if you take them from the sources you encounter, like articles or books you find interesting. You can add phrases in ready to use form instead of just words (e.g. 'I'm interested in astronomy' or 'I find ancient history fascinating' - of course if these are true about you). The amount of time spent on reviewing depends on the number of new cards per day, so if someone has less time or patience, even three or five new words are ok. Naturally it cannot be considered the one and only method for everyone as such thing doesn't exist. Different people have different possibilities, experience, ways of learning. I use Anki intensively and it really helps. I have words, phrases, quotes and questions (the last are not translation but e.g. How tall is the wall of a Roman camp? - It's 10 feet tall.; both in Latin). The goal is also important, as professional translation may require the knowledge of specific terms and vocabulary. I strongly recommend learning Anki and using it for language learning.

I now spend most of time either just ingesting content (written or audio), translating (read/write/read out loud), or talking to a tutor. **@ancalagonyt** (👍0 · 2025-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tCBbGbRvkGo&lc=UgxJu6rsdU9rtQZiYPJ4AaABAg
  Other than your preferred method, which sounds good, all of these points are based on misconceptions.  I appreciate you saying all this, even though I basically disagree with all of it, because it was so clearly and specifically set out.  
  
  First, making flashcards is learning time.  Typing a word exposes you to that word and its spelling.  Including a sample sentence (probably the sentence where you encountered the word) ensures that you have context every time you review it, and involves reading that sentence at least once, if not analyzing the sentence in detail.  Putting a definition in makes you look it up and summarize the meaning of the word in your own words.
  
  Second, you don't need to make flashcards if you download a premade deck.  It takes literally zero time to download a deck someone else spent time on.
  
  Third, if adding new cards becomes an addiction, that's not a problem for learning, since adding new cards is learning time.
  
  Fourth, reviewing old cards only becomes a chore if you don't know how or why this can happen.  If you start of going as fast as you can on a day when you have lots of energy and free time, then by definition, you're going too fast, and once the reviews build up, you won't be able to keep up anymore.
  
  There's a saying in computer programming: never write a program as cleverly as you can, because by definition, you're not smart enough to debug it.  The same thing applies to an SRS, since you're committing to new cards plus reviews, and you're committing to doing about the same amount every day, even on days where you're busy.  If you start out doing as much as you can on a day when it's just new cards, by definition, you're doing too much, and it will overwhelm you, and then you'll stop.
  
  Don't be afraid of going slow, either.  Two cards per day, every single day, is 730 words per year.
  
  Fifth, learning words out of context is fine.  When you see those words in context, you'll learn new nuances and meanings, and when you see other words you don't know, you'll have a better chance to learn those words, since this one is part of that word's context.
  
  Sixth, if you put an example sentence in a card you make or if you have a premade deck with example sentences in it, that puts the flashcard back in context.
  
  Seventh, cards can be made with a particular context in mind.  If you've got a set of cards that relate to a particular paragraph or chapter, you can read and/or listen to that text, which helps with those words, but also helps with understanding that text.
  
  Eighth, flashcards don't need to take up hours of time, nor do they have to be divorced from learning words in context.  They help you learn words in context, because you know more of the words in the context.
  
  Ninth, flashcards aren't taking time away from natural language learning with experience in the language.  For cards you make yourself, you're doing that while you're reading or listening.  For decks you download, you're preparing to meet those words in the wild, and when you do, you'll be better ready to absorb information about that word, or better able to understand the context to help with other words.
  
  Tenth, you don't need to make a perfect Anki card, and a good one won't take long.  You only need the word, correctly spelled, with a gloss or definition that isn't wrong.  Preferably you also want an example sentence, which at most takes copying and pasting it from the context where you found it.  Spending whole seconds to focus on a word, its spelling and pronunciation, its meaning, and an example sentence is (1) not a long time and (2) is time spent on experience in the language.
  
  Eleventh, if you're making a large deck with hundreds of cards for yourself, you aren't going to be spending several minutes per card.  You will put in enough time to know how to make a high quality card in the smallest amount of time possible.
  
  If you're making a large deck with thousands of cards for other people, chances are you're using a program to help you do it, whether you wrote the program or someone else did.  The program will do the majority of the work.  
  
  Twelfth, the size of your Anki decks can't spiral out of control, because the size of an Anki deck has no cost.
  
  Thirteenth, you can take a day off, if you need to.  Or a week.
  
  You'll have a backlog, but that's not a big deal.  You can turn off new cards, set new cards to a lower level, or turn on the setting that makes the reviews go first before you see new cards.
  
  Fourteenth, though everything you said about language being a network and context being important is true, flashcards still help.  Flashcards tell you about the nodes in that network.  The more you understand the nodes, the easier it is to understand the network.
  
  If you put context back in, by making your own flashcards, using example sentences, and finding the words you studied in the wild, this also helps learning.
  
  Fifteenth, while SRSs are about the benefits of repeating things and spacing out the repetitions, they also do the spacing in an exponential decay.  While this is not impossible to do by hand, it's easier to do by computer.
  
  The system of reviewing a piece of text you describe is spaced evenly.  Since you're not learning the text itself, this is not a problem.  But it isn't using the power of spaced repetitions to the full, since the spacing is all the same.
  
  You could combine the power of spaced repetitions by learning words in an SRS that are in a particular text, then using the text in the even spacing as described.  Reading the words in context would help you learn and understand the individual words, and knowing the words would help you understand and learn from the text.

  I use it like this:
  1. Open Excel and write down all kinds of things you would talk about in an fictive conversation you'd have with a friend or family memeber. Also write about what happend to you that day (especially emotional things).
  2. After about 50 sentences, I'll just paste them into ChatGPT. To help Chat GPT I also would sometimes help by explaining the context of the sentence in brackets. Of couse: Don't post anything too personal!
  3. Then I copy the translation and post it to another column next to the old one in Excel. Copy the old (native language) and the new column (foreign language) into a text file to import them all in one shot into Anki.
  4. Depending on the language I then let Awesome TTS create a voice example for all of the imported sentences. Also evenlabs is very good for this but it's a pain in the ass because you have to do it sentence by sentence.

**@StillAliveAndKicking_** (👍0 · 2024-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tCBbGbRvkGo&lc=UgyiOyoAmYFmXkVsTep4AaABAg
  Your arguments are of course valid, but I think there is a place for Anki when used with care. I use Anki for French (B2+) and German (six months learning) and I find it extremely useful. You say that it wastes time entering words. I enjoy entering words, it forces me to look more closely at the word, including spelling. Often the act of writing down a word or phrase can help memorisation. You say that it is a chore to practice with. I enjoy the daily practice, but that is clearly my subjective experience, and if someone does not enjoy it, then obviously they should look elsewhere. You say that it presents words out of context. Yes it does if used poorly. For a noun, add a note to remove ambiguity. Thus a fan could be an admirer, an adherent, or a ventilator. In the case of a verb, the word on its own is often useless, so I add a sentence showing the usage. I find Anki especially good to practice German grammar. Thus I add sentences such as “Ich sollte einige dieser Gefühle niederschreiben”. The great polyglot Kató Lomb was a fan of learning phrases. For me Anki is a small part of my learning process. One big advantage is that it also allows me to learn words I do not hear often but want to remember. Thus names of birds: L’allouette des champs, la hirondelle, le héron, le merle, le moineau, la pie, le pivert, le rapace, le faison, le pigeon. Or tools: le marteau, le rabot, le ciseau, la scie, la perceuse électrique. And so on. I cannot find audio input that uses those words, but they are part of my soul, so to speak. And those words are not ambiguous. I use Anki to get words into my brain, and then I listen to a lot of audio input, and for most words, that teaches me the proper usage, including the context, and the register. But without Anki I won’t understand what I hear.

**@jennifer255** (👍0 · 2023-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tCBbGbRvkGo&lc=UgyjxpXzGF0LVroVCrJ4AaABAg
  While I think (physical) flashcards are great (if they need context, I'll just add it in brackets. i.e., [sun]light, light[weight] - Being a computer programmer, I'm a terrible artist, so no pictures...), I also don't like apps for a few reason -
  
  1 - It feels too gamey (some have multiple choice, mix-and-match, etc. I feel like that over-complicates the process.). Constantly reminding me (filling up my inbox) to learn a rolling set of words is just too spammy as well.
  
  2 - I like holding a physical card in my hand (or, at the very least, a side-by-side list of words), and I can mix and match as needed, without being limited by what the app can and can not do. The only pre-made cards I've purchased (and this was around the year 2000, well before apps or YouTube) were Tuttle Kanji Cards when I was learning Japanese, and I'd learn 5-10 at a time. I'd review them at my own leisure, too. I will have to give Anki's flashcard list from a movie thing a try, though. That sounds interesting.
  
  3 - I prefer thematic learning, not the sometimes random words I see on apps. By the time I get to the 201/202 (B1 equivalent) level, sometimes late 102 (A2), I might try and learn from short stories. I find if I listen to an enjoyable song about 7 times or so, I start recognizing words. Flash cards just reinforces that I've learned those words. 
  
  
  The way I prefer using flashcards is - (To use the CEFR equivalent levels) -
  
  A1/A2 - Build a flashcard list of words learned in that lesson's theme (i.e., greetings, interrogatives, months/time, classroom objects, colors, etc.) with a few examples phrases/grammar. That lets me start to substitute any new vocabulary I've learned, which then reinforces words in the example sentences. Even writing down the example sentence is practicing writing in that language.
  
  B1/B2 - Flashcards would come from themed reading/listening. Say I read a children's book, and there were 50 new words, I'd use the 5-10 words-at-a-time method (i.e. 1. 2 (2 times) 1-2 (quickly 3 times), then 3.4.5. (2 times, then quickly 3 times), then repeat the whole set. I'd re-read the book, and any words that I still don't understand, I'd put the cards into the "reinforce" pile. I'd probably start to wean myself off of flashcards at this point, and start trying to describe the new words using words I already know (kind of like fractions in math where you get the "least common denominator".
  
  C1/C2 - I am not at this level, but I'd probably start using a dictionary in the target language at this point. If you need to learn the "last" 12,000 words (4,000 for C1, 8,000 for C2), those are probably going to be too much for flashcards.

  I really think we lack solid scientific data on this topic. Ideally we would have two sufficiently large groups of learners of the same target language, and the members of one would use anki for a fixed amount of time every day when they others would be devoting that time every day. Then after 1, 2, 5, 10 years we could see how there proficiency evolved and compare the two groups. 
  Since such a study it is unlikely to come out soon, I would be okay with trusting the feedback of someone that has learned comparable languages in terms of difficulty, one with each method.
  I think the key to remembering words is to experience an emotional committing experience with that word. It might be harder to do with anki but not impossible. In any case, I would think it's best in that regard that one makes their own cards. By emotionally committing I mean learning a word in a topic you are genuinely interested in, or a word that you would need to use in a real situation.
  I think that Anki could be used effectively to learn the core vocabulary of a language if you take the time to create context cards (e.g. cloze deletions) that are inspired by events of your own life that carry as much emotional strength as possible. Then when you process the card you remember the event. Also it's best to have several cards for the same word, especially for abstract concepts (not really needed for words like 'dog' or 'apple' for instance)

**@luuk777w** (👍1 · 2024-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tCBbGbRvkGo&lc=UgyVKKCNH0G4jW79U154AaABAg
  I highly disagree. I use Anki, but in a totally different way.
  First, I choose a piece of content. Usually and EasyGreek video (I am learning Greek). 
  Then, I will make a transcription of the video, and split it in sections of 30 sections.
  This is my first encounter with the piece of content and just watching the video, and listening, and typing every word already does a lot.
  My next step is to retrieve each unique word from each section that I do not know yet. I have written some software for this to do this for me.
  This software returns a text document with lists of words, each containing new words for me.
  
  With this list, I go to ChatGPT for which I have created a special prompt. I give ChatGPT the list together with the section of transcript for context. ChatGPT is instructed to highly take context in to account, and combine words in small sentences to make sure it does not lose meaning and stay logical. A lot of times multiple words together have one meaning. 
  This gives me a list of flashcards that I can import into Anki. Once a week I add new flashcards to Anki taking about 10 minutes.
  
  After I have done my flashcard session, I go and watch the video again until the point what I have learned so far and I will speak a long with the video. I do this a couple of times.
  
  Doing this keeps the context, and makes the flashcards not meaningless.

**@laurencedavenport543** (👍2 · 2024-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tCBbGbRvkGo&lc=Ugy1yqI2PApb4oD7I3J4AaABAg
  I am so glad it is not just me that doesn't get on with Anki. The horror of seeing 200 cards in your review box is a nightmare for ADHD learners like myself. Luca is absolutely right - if you don't keep on top of the cards, they keep piling up. I love Luca's method of reviewing the same words in context using different methods: it keeps everything fresh. An added bonus to learning through comprehensible language is that high frequency words are the vocabularly that are reviewed the most: the clue is in the name. This means that I don't have to keep reviewing words like "roundabout" or "traffic cone" on a flashcard that I made during an exercise on giving directions. Instead, I would pick up "left", "right", "ahead" in different contexts. The is how I learnt that "tomar la pimera a la derecha", "seguir derecho", and "los derechos de autor" were all different things. With Anki I would have drilled the first and missed the others - especially "seguir derecho" which is obvious when reading a dialogue with accompanying map but not so in isolation as a flashcard.

    ↳ **@nikolaikai940** (👍0 · 2026-04-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tCBbGbRvkGo&lc=UgyWV_NeFXRoJR4PX0N4AaABAg.AOSOcSaw2lwAUxqzoCfja8
      > very surprising no one has created the ideal version of Anki yet, all of [Anki's] problems are quite simple to solve
      That's because none of the criticisms leveraged against Anki are actually Anki problems, but just people using it inefficiently. There's nothing for Anki to solve or become more ideal. It's a bit like blaming a blank canvas for people drawing stick figures on it and wondering why the "perfect canvas" that makes everyone paint like J.S. Sargent hasn't been invented yet.
      
      That's after all what Anki is, a blank canvas for flashcards with as much freedom to create whatever kind of card you want with it. You can make the shittiest nonsensical flashcards with it, or outright masterpieces in terms of efficiency.
      
      Your app where a card shows several examples and has multimedia content to go along with it, all that is possible in Anki as well since it has full audio/video/image support and Anki cards are formatted in HTML/CSS, you could make each card an entire fully fledged webpage if you felt like it.
      
      And for the criticism in this video...
      1. Creating flash cards wastes time
      Not really, at least for Japanese there's specialized extensions that create entire cards including definitions and example sentences with just 1-2 clicks on a word on a webpage. And if you take your time to create cards manually I'd argue that actually is learning time, since you're actively spending time with each word looking up definitions, looking for example sentences, listening to audio samples to include etc.
      
      2. Creating cards can be addictive
      So can anything, that's not an Anki specific problem. Just don't get addicted.
      
      3. Reviewing can become a chore
      Not if you moderate yourself and pick a reasonable amount of new cards to learn per day and if you do get overwhelmed with reviews, just drop the new cards to 0 for a couple days until you've cleared the backlog and then set the new cards per day to something lower than the number that caused the pileup, wash rinse repeat until you find a sweet spot that works for you.
      
      4. Missing context
      Again, not an Anki problem. Remember, blank canvas, you are in full control to include as much or as little context for each word. As I said, you can have a card show just the word, or make a full multi-media webpage for each word with audio, video, animated GIFs, images and links to websites that provide more context, all up to you.
      
      
      Same goes for pre-made decks, there are really simple ones but also those that come with hundreds of megabytes of pictures and audio. And if you do use a pre-made deck and find some cards have not enough context, or it doesn't click with you, simple, just edit the card and replace what's there with something that makes sense to you. That's the fun thing, even with pre-made decks you retain full control and can make all the edits in the world.

  I agree with every criticism you have about Anki.  I will therefore use Anki carefully keeping these criticisms in mind.  (Luca is probalby thinking: This is NOT why I made this video!).  One big problem is I don't have your discipline to to sit down and work through material thoroughly over time on my own with pen and paper.  I think you offer a very valid alternative to Anki for some people.  But for me the only realistic alternative I have to not using Anki is to just immerse (basically read read read read) with no rote or focused learning at all.  However, I think it's more efficient to combine focused rote memorization of specific vocabulary with immersion.  The problem is when your Anki "addiction" interferes with immersion due to all of your criticisms.  I almost feel like I should write down all of your criticisms and post it where I can see it to make sure I don't fall victim.
  
  edit I think the biggest trap many SRS adopters fall into is into thinking they need SRS to remember EVERY word they want to learn in the target language.  I know I fall into thinking this even though I know otherwise.  But if you immerse you will absolutely absorb vocabulary without drilling it in Anki.  You don't need to put everything into Anki.  You get it for "free." in a sense - just relax, use Anki sparingly, and it will help you instead of holding you back.  If you spend too much time on Anki instead of immersing then Anki WILL hold your learning back - you will still advance of course but words only learned in Anki and not encountered in immersion are weakly learned.  Don't let Anki keep you from immersing.  If at the end of the day you are often saying to yourself that you didn't get much if any immersion but at least you got your Anki reviews done then it's probably holding you back.

  How much time to spend on repetition and how many new words to learn per day is up to you, all this can be set up in the app. But this process is quite simple and makes self-organization and discipline easier. Personally, I don’t mind meditating for a while during this process.
  You don’t need to create cards manually if you don’t want to. This can all be done automatically. You need to mine words from a video resource on the Internet. Thus, Anki doesn't take words out of context. That is, you should only use Anki in conjunction with immersion in the language by watching a bunch of videos and texts on the Internet. For example, you can use Yomitan and ASBplayer in order to easily work with videos and subtitles, automatically creating new cards for Anki based on the words you come across. No time is spent on creating a card at all, time is spent only on watching videos and parsing unfamiliar words.
  Anki is really complicated, but personally I spent 2-3 days to figure it out, it’s not that much, and it’s worth it.
  And again, Anki should only be used with language immersion to mine the exact words you encounter.

**@nguyenkhanhhailinh1721** (👍0 · 2026-06-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tCBbGbRvkGo&lc=UgwnKpn4Ng7ZTBOPp7B4AaABAg
  As someone who didn't like anki at first, but now uses it a lot, I feel like I need to address a few things in case someone new stumble upon this video like I did
  1. Most seasoned Anki users don't recommend making your own flash cards when starting out, we mostly use pre made high quality decks for  the most common couple of thousand words (for example, for Japanese learning, there's the Kaishi 1.5 and the core 2k 3k decks)
  
  This eliminate both the time and effort intensive downside of Anki and gets you to straight learning, they also contain example sentences, with native audio and proper images.
  
  This allow for a more broad and nuance understanding of the word in real life context, which avoid narrow understanding
  
  2. Anki's SRS system is automatic, but it is completely based on your own input, not random, if you remember a word, Anki pushes it back further in the review queue, and if you don't, Anki knows to show it to you more frequently. The purpose is to only (mostly) show you words that you don't remember, which cuts down on the time of going over vocab you already know. This is why Anki's regarded as one of the most effective vocab learning tool

  Whilst I do agree with you that there are better methods to learn vocabulary in a foreign language than with Anki, I disagree with many of the points you've made in this video. In particular, that making flashcards wastes learning time. I've spent years using Anki flashcards to learn languages and I've always considered making the flashcards to be some of my most valuable learning time. For much of my Anki career I've gone by some variation of a rule that prohibits me from using any language but the target language itself on the flashcard. This forced me to come up with creative ways to express the meaning of words and phrases using either photos, or the language itself, which in itself was a valuable learning opportunity for me. In fact, I often found that even if I never reviewed those cards again after making them and initially learning them, much of the vocabulary would stick in my brain.
  I also ensure that I include context on my flashcards. You're right in that this did extend the time required for me to create cards, however it forced me to read material in the language in order to find an appropriate example of that word in the context that I required, deepening my initial understanding of the vocabulary even further, before even having review the Anki card even once.
  After all of this, each review of that card was a reminder of everything I had learned whilst making the card.
  Great video though. I have not tried your bidirectional translation method so perhaps I try that next and then rethink my opinion on Anki.

  Sorry, but you're objectively misinformed. Also, there are studies in foreign language learning which show that flashcards can be beneficial. For example, Paul Nation, a top academic linguist, recommends the use of flashcards, it's part of the "four strands to language learning". 
  
  The problem of your video is that you focused on the bad ways to use Anki thinking those are the only ways. It would have been more useful and informed if you had searched about better ways to use Anki and still inform people about the bad ways. It could be a video about how people shouldn't use Anki. There is no scientific support to say that learners shouldn't use flashcards at all. This is nonsense.
  
  1. There are high quality pre-made Anki decks. 
  2. You don't necessarily have to make cards to use Anki.
  3. Chores can also bring good results. "Piling up" is not completely true either, you can set the quantity of cards you'd like to review. 
  4. High quality Anki decks have context, images, example sentences. Even so, no one should use them in isolation. 
  5. Because you don't find Anki brain-friendly, it doesn't mean others won't. If people find motivation with Anki, that's where they should go for. 
  6. People don't have to "find audio files".  Anki supports high-quality naturalistic text-to-speech software.

      @vaxrvaxr  A while back I did a quick and dirty estimate of how long it'd take before the natural repetition rate I got through extensive reading was higher than the repetition rate in SM-2 (so, any SRS using SM-2). After that break-even point, it stands to reason that keeping the flashcard running no longer serves any purpose. I had to make a lot of assumptions for that estimate, and a lot of them aren't necessarily realistic, but it was just to get a broad idea. And what I found was that if I read 1h a day, the break-even point for the 15k most frequent words occurs after only about 10 days or so. After those 10 days, I encounter those 15k words more frequently in extensive reading than I do in the SRS, so there's no point keeping the flashcards. In practice that break-even point would be different of course, but yeah, I just mention it to give an idea of just how short the time span where SRS is actually useful can be. My hunch is that the people who get trapped into having too many reviews just aren't deleting their cards even long after they stopped serving any purpose. I can understand keeping a card running for a few months, but at some point it really does become counterproductive to keep them running. And that point is probably a lot earlier than a lot of SRS users think.

      @JohnnyLynnLee  You make a fair point - all my experience is with relatively similar languages to English with a bunch of cognates. 
      
      Given that amassing vocab is the #1 hurdle to overcome on the road to C1/C2, learning a related language gives you a huge head start for sure. Italian, for example, has at least 5000 closely related words that are often guessable. Learning that number of words in a remote language would take years, as you point out. 
      
      And it must be very difficult to react with any kind of meaningful material until you have at least 500 words or so.
      
      I guess that a lot depends on your temperament. Personally I find working through decks crushingly boring and demotivating so I'd never stay the course.  
      
      I need something that's more interactive and creative. My current approach to output involves building scenarios, writing scripts and acting them out. I use this to drill grammar patterns as well. This is actual fun - even learning those damned romance verb systems is tolerable.
      
      If I ever tackle a remote language I'll have to find another way. I'm pretty sure it could be done.
      
      What I've learned is that people have very different learning styles and there is no "One True Way". I lot of the YouTube gurus seem very dogmatic and assume that what works for them must be optimal for everyone else - they can get positively abusive if you dare to question their dogmatic assertions (translation is damaging, grammar is a waste of time etc etc).

      @anastasif  Good question. I used it for Japanese conjuga5ions and stuff, since  Japanese is an agglutinative language. And, as a Brazilian, I also recommend it for people with trouble with conjugations (and even my Vietnamese students learning English, since Vietnamese has no conjugations at all and even conjugations in English are hard as hell to them).
      
      Instead of starting from the VERB and putting all the conjugations (or cases) think of the conjugation (or case) as A WORD in and of itself. 
      
      for instance.
      
      In Japanese "to go" is 行く. But "I want to go" is 行きたい. The "volitional" form. You conjugate the verbs to show you WANT to do that action. 
      
      Well, think of this part "たい" as a WORD, like "I want to (do an action)." And use 2 or 3 examples of verbs modified by this "たい" thing. Kinda of REVERSE of people would do. Try it. It work miracles for me.
      
      Stop thinking "my God there is dozes of forms to conjugate ONE ver. Thing of conjugations as WORDS that ATTACH to verbs anc dhance them. Leanr the cases or conjugations are separate entities, one by one and FORGET about the noumns or verbs for now. And in OTHER cards youdo think of the verbs in their basic form ("dictionary forma" in Japanese. In time your brain you connect the dots.

      @anastasif  "But I'm afraid that you don't realize how vast Russian nouns and adjectives declension is!". Again the problem is that you are ASSUMING you have to learn them all at once. I tried Russian for 2 months before dropping it in favor of Vietnamese, which I've been in for more than 3 years now. 
      
      See how I was approaching it. Besides making cards from "A Frequency Dictionary of Russian: core vocabulary for learners" whatever the word and example sentence it was there, I'd open an article in Russian. Than I'd break down sentence by sentence, starting from the opening sentence, mining for words. I would add whatever word I felt it was at "my level" from each sentence, in WHATEVER form they appeared in that PARTICULAR sentence. I would consult what case it was in a site that gives you that for a word and put on the card that was X word in X case. And done! I wouldn't care how that word changes in OTHER cases. I WOULD  for sure see again that word in some other case if I'd keep doing it. At the beginning you may spend even one hour in less than one paragraph doing it. That's fine. The more you do, as the months go by, the faster you go.  Even only in 2 months it happened for me to encounter the same word in different declensions. When that happened I would look up ONLY for that declension that I was dealing with in THAT sentence that appeared to me in THAT article. Eventually you WILL run up in ALL declensions, applied to different words. You will FORGET most of them, and look it up again. that's normal too. If you keep doing it you'll learn all the declensions. To the point where if you see a new word in a new article in ONE particular declension you already can guess 3, 4, 5 other declensions for that word. Focus only on the WORD AT HAND. What that particular word mean, in which declension it is. The meaning of the word, how that particular declension works, what it does. Don think, like, "what are the other declensions for this word?"  To understand THAT word in THAT sentence, to understand what's being said in THAT article you just need this one. If you keep doing it you'll meet each and every declension, with TIME. It would take months, years, doing it everyday. It's not a thing you can learn al at once. Like characters in Japanese and Chinese. Comprehension hypothesis, you know? You are trying ONLY to understand THAT sentence, in THAT paragraph, on THAT article. One at a time.

      In simple terms. don't try to learn the declension and an example sentence with and example word. Lear A SENTENCE. and learn whatever is used in THAT sentence. No matter if the enemy that THOUSANDS on the other side and they had only 300 dudes. To get to them on that tight space it would be ONE Persian against ONE Spartan.

      @Ernie7695  I'm not convinced that it does take longer - with a bit of imagination you can be working intensively with new patterns and vocab in much more enjoyable and stimulating ways.
      
      I'm very far from an expert on language learning, but I am something of an expert on academic study technique - and in that scenario flashcards are a pretty woeful method, despite their popularity.
      
      Learning random atomic facts out of context goes against everything we know about how the brain learns. FAR better to use mind-maps to work with networks of facts embedded in a rich and meaningful context.
      
      I can't see why the same principles shouldn't apply to language learning. With the techniques I've picked up over the years even grammar become fun and productive.
      
      I guess we shouldn't be dogmatic - some people seem to enjoy working with flashcards and do pretty well. But many, many people fail, so it's good that people like Luca are offering alternatives.

**@evangelizacaoespiritainfantil** (👍9 · 2023-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XIga6wpPbo0&lc=UgyHBG7Pl-BDJ82Al-l4AaABAg
  Serene - calm, peaceful, and tranquil; free from disturbance or agitation.
  Stunning - extremely impressive or attractive; causing wonder or amazement.
  Picturesque - visually attractive or scenic, resembling a picture or painting; charming or quaint.
  Desolate - deserted, abandoned, or devoid of life; bleak, lonely, and uninhabited.
  Unspoiled - in its original, natural, or pristine state; not spoiled, altered, or corrupted.
  Pristine - in perfect condition or untouched state; clean, fresh, and pure.
  Tranquil - calm, quiet, and peaceful; free from disturbance or commotion.
  Vibrant - full of life, energy, and activity; dynamic, lively, and colorful.
  Homey - cozy, comfortable, and inviting, with a warm and familiar atmosphere.
  Bustling - full of activity, noise, or excitement; lively and busy with people or activity.
  Renowned - widely known or celebrated for a particular quality or achievement; famous or esteemed.
  Cosmopolitan - sophisticated, worldly, and diverse; characteristic of a major city with a global outlook.
  Walkable - easily accessible or suitable for walking; pedestrian-friendly.
  Overcrowded - excessively crowded or packed with people or objects; lacking space or room.
  Spacious - large, roomy, and ample in size or extent; not cramped or confined.
  Charming - delightful, attractive, and pleasant in an endearing way; full of charisma or appeal.
  Quaint - attractively old-fashioned or picturesque; possessing a unique or unusual charm.
  Iconic - widely recognized and regarded as a symbol or representation of something; emblematic.
  Contemporary - current, modern, or up-to-date; existing or occurring in the present time.
  Majestic - grand, impressive, and awe-inspiring; having dignity, splendor, or regal beauty.
  Gaudy - flashy, showy, and ostentatious in a tasteless or excessive way; overly bright or garish.
  Dilapidated - in a state of disrepair, decay, or deterioration; run-down or shabby.
  Out-of-the-way - secluded, remote, or off the main path; not easily accessible or well-known.
  Off the beaten path/track - away from the usual or well-traveled route; unconventional or uncommon.
  Godforsaken - desolate, forsaken, or isolated; lacking signs of human habitation or care.

  1. Most Common Functional Words (33.5% of essay content)
  These are everyday words essential for sentence structure:
  the, to, of, in, that, are, this, they (2:04 - 2:27)
  
  2. High-Frequency Topic-Specific Keywords
  Commonly used in Task 2 topics like education and health:
  people, children, time, companies, parents, life, school, health, employees, diet (3:59 - 4:29)
  
  3. Essential Linking Words (Cohesive Devices)
  Instead of using complex or obscure linkers, successful students stick to functional, clear options:
  in conclusion, however, although, for instance, as a result, therefore (6:27 - 6:33)
  
  4. Examples of "C1/C2" Vocabulary
  The speaker notes that even higher-level vocabulary is usually functional and topic-specific rather than "fancy" or rare:
  accountable, adolescent, advocate, allocate, aspirations, assault (12:13 - 12:20)
  
  Key Strategy Summary
  The speaker advises against memorizing lists of complex words (1:42). Instead, focus on:
  Accuracy: Using simple words correctly (1:12).
  Existing Vocabulary: Leveraging the words you already know (1:30).
  Topic Specificity: Using words that actually fit the subject matter rather than trying to impress with complexity (1:47, 4:58).

**@bahauddinchishte** (👍282 · 2024-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0-mr-rtWssk&lc=Ugyp5mFVrepzK9jTLxZ4AaABAg
  Here is a list of words covered in the video along with an example for each word:
  
  Ineffable: The pig's delight was ineffable when she got engaged to a millionaire. (This means something is so extreme it cannot be described in words.)
  Succinct: Her text response was succinct and left no doubt on his mind on where he stood. (This means something is short and to the point.)
  Mitigate: I'm trying to mitigate my coffee addiction by switching to decaf. (This means to try to make something less severe.)
  Benevolent: The benevolent beaver shed his bounty of wood with his neighbors. (This means kind or having goodwill.)
  Elucidate: No one could elucidate the concepts of chemistry better than Professor Buck. (This means to explain something clearly.)
  Discord: Disputes over how to spend money caused intense discord with the newlyweds. (This means disagreement or lack of harmony.)
  Nuance: The subtle nuance of wearing socks with sandals can only be understood by our generation. (This means a slight detail.)
  Pragmatic: The goat's pragmatic solution to selling donuts was to advertise them on his horns. (This means being practical and logical.)
  Obsolete: Mr. Kus realized his calculator was obsolete when he found a new one. (This means outdated or no longer relevant.)
  Altruistic: Mr. Box was skeptical when the cat claimed to be selling authentic dinosaur bones (This means selfless or caring about others without thinking about yourself.)
  Innocuous: Despite the pup's innocuous appearance, he was known to break dishes and eat homework. (This means harmless.)
  Abysmal: He was shocked when his test grades came back with an absolutely abysmal grade. (This means very bad or poor.)
  Animosity: The animosity between my pets was a constant source of chaos in my house. (This means hatred or dislike.)
  Affluent: The affluent family of the Frog Prince posed for the holiday portrait. (This means wealthy or rich.)
  Eccentric: My bestie is a little eccentric with her fashion choices but she is still a blast to hang out with. (This means strange or odd.)
  Eloquent: The best man gave an eloquent speech at his best friend's wedding. (This means speaking beautifully and clearly.)
  Lament: Susan lamented not having studied for the SAT more seriously. (This means to feel regret or sorrow.)
  Stark: I arrived at what was supposed to be my dream destination, I was shocked at the stark and desolate landscape. (This means empty and without any decoration or features.)
  Ubiquitous: Cell phones are ubiquitous these days. (This means being everywhere or extremely common.)
  Palpable: The excitement in the crowd of fans was palpable when the band walked out on stage. (This means you can almost touch or feel the feeling, even though it is not physical.)
  Ambivalent: When he proposed, she suddenly felt quite ambivalent. (This means unsure or having mixed feelings.)
  Hinder: My work was hindered by an unexpected herd of oblivious goats. (This means to slow something down or prevent it from happening.)
  Oblivious: To hinder is to hold back, it's to prevent, it's to limit one's ability to do something. Bonus word in this sentence if you didn't catch it is oblivious and that is to be completely unaware.
  Tenuous: After the lack of rain, the state of Farmer Brown's farm was tenuous to say the least. (This means weak or fragile.)
  Lucrative: Selling bamboo juice proved to be a lucrative venture right next to Panda daycare. (This means profitable or making a lot of money.)
  
  PS. Don't think I am wasting my time, I used Gemeni to write it 😂

      @bellooluwatobi4813  Of course , For the writing task one , please make sure to take notes accurately and mention all the points in the lecture , it's really useful to use a template , you don't have to come up with new ideas or topics , you just have to write what is stated in the lecture and the passage using the template, no need for extra complicated vocab , just make sure to write at least 280 words + little or no mistakes ( replace any word you're not sure of its spelling ) , so to sum this up - Mention all the points - Word count - use a good template with different contradictory words in each paragraph -revise and correct or change any complex vocab

      @bellooluwatobi4813  task two is much easier I think .
      Use an introductory sentence with your opinion , add one more sentence of agreement or disagreement with the other two students , Mention a reason/ or example supporting your choice or opinion 
      use connecting words or adjunctive ( however , so that , on the contrary , having said that , otherwise , in addition to ) something like that , revise and correct any errors or mistakes ( al least in 1-2) minutes 
      \
